This embedding is not unique, and depends on the choice of a unit vector $\tau\in \overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}$ such that $\Theta=\lbrace\alpha \in \Delta\mid \alpha(\tau)>0\rbrace$. Given a flag $f\in \mathcal{F}_\Theta$ a a maximal flat $F\subset \mathbb{X}$ we say that $f$ is in the boundary of $F$ if for one of these embeddings $f$ is mapped inside $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F\subset \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} \mathbb{X}$. label: prop:Tits angle
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tau \in \overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}$  be a unit vector such that $\lbrace \alpha \in \Delta \mid \alpha (\tau)>0\rbrace =\Theta$.
Up to acting by $G$, since $f$ and $f^\text{opp}$ are transverse we can assume that the stabilizer of $f$ in $G$ is equal to the stabilizer of the class of the ray $t \mapsto \exp(\tau t)o$ in $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} \mathbb{X}$ and the stabilizer of $f^\text{opp}$ is equal to the stabilizer of the class of the ray $t \mapsto \exp(-\tau t)o$.

\medskip

Let $f'$ be the flag opposite to $f$ in a flat $F$ containing $f$ and $g$ in its boundary. The relative position of the pair $(f',g)$ is therefore $[w_0 w_1]$. We consider the $1$-parameter subgroup $(g_t)$ of $G$ consisting of transvections along a geodesic in the flat $F$ whose limit is $f'$. This group fixes $(f',f,g)$ but since $f$ and $f^\text{opp}$ are transverse then $g_t\cdot f^\text{opp}$ converges to $f'$. This fact is the so-called North-South dynamics of semi-simple elements in semisimple Lie groups. Hence since the pairs $g_t\cdot(f^\text{opp},g)$ converge to $(f',g)$, we have $ [w_0w_1]\leq [w_2]$.

label: prop: volume density along K-orbits
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: volume density along K-orbits}
    The volume measure $\operatorname{Leb}$ on $\mathbb{X}$, up to a multiplicative constant, satisfies for every integrable function $f$ on $\mathbb{X}$:
    $$\int_\mathbb{X} f(x)\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Leb} =\int_{\mathfrak{a}^+} \left(\int_{K/M}f(kM \cdot e^\tau o) \mathrm{d}\text{Haar}(kM)\right) \mathrm{d}\mu_\mathfrak{a}(\tau).$$
    Here $\text{Haar}$ is the Haar probability measure on $K/M$, which is naturally identified with the orbit $K\cdot e^\tau o$ for all regular $\tau\in \mathfrak{a}^+$ (hence for almost every $\tau \in \mathfrak{a}^+$), and $\mu_\mathfrak{a}$ is the measure $\prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} \left(2\sinh(\alpha (\tau))\right)^{m_\alpha}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Leb}_\mathfrak{a}(\tau)$ with $\operatorname{Leb}_\mathfrak{a}$ the volume measure on the Euclidean space $\mathfrak{a}$ and $m_\alpha$ is the dimension of the root space $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha$ associated with $\alpha\in \Sigma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For almost every point $x \in \mathbb{X}$ the vector-valued distance $\vec{d}(o,x)$ is regular.
At such a regular point, $T_x\mathbb{X}$ splits orthogonally as $T_x((K\cdot x) \oplus T_xF$ where $F$ is the unique flat containing the base point $o\in \mathbb{X}$  and $x\in \mathbb{X}$. 
The invariant volume measure $\operatorname{Leb}$ therefore splits locally as a product measure of the Lebesgue measure $\operatorname{Leb}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ on $F \simeq \mathfrak{a}$ and a $K$-invariant measure on $K\cdot x$. 
Hence there is some $\Phi \colon \mathfrak{a}^+ \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ relating this measure to the Haar probability measure on $K/M$. 

\medskip

We look at the orbit map $\phi \colon K/M \to K \cdot x$, where $x = e^v o$. 
Note that $K$ and hence $K/M$ come equipped with a natural Riemannian metric coming from the Killing form of $\mathfrak{g}$.
The determinant of the differential of $\phi$ is constant and equal to the determinant of the linear map:
$$ k\in \mathfrak{k}/\mathfrak{m} \mapsto  \pi_\mathfrak{p}(e^{\mathrm{ad}_v} k)=\sinh(\mathrm{ad}_v) k\in \mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{a}.$$
Here $\pi_\mathfrak{p}$ is the projection onto $\mathfrak{p}$ coming from the $\mathfrak{k}\oplus \mathfrak{p}$ decomposition.
This linear map takes $\mathfrak{k}_\alpha = (\mathfrak{g}_\alpha\oplus \mathfrak{g}_{-\alpha}) \cap \mathfrak{k}$ isomorphically to $\mathfrak{p}_\alpha = (\mathfrak{g}_\alpha\oplus \mathfrak{g}_{-\alpha}) \cap \mathfrak{p}$ for all (positive) roots $\alpha$.
For $X \in \mathfrak{g}_\alpha$ the map is given by
    \[ X+ \theta X_\alpha \mapsto \sinh(\alpha(v)) (X- \theta X_\alpha), \]
where $\theta$ is the Cartan involution corresponding to $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{k}\oplus \mathfrak{p}$.
Therefore the determinant is equal to :
$$ \prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} \sinh(\alpha (v))^{m_\alpha} $$
where $m_\alpha$ denotes the dimension of the root space $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha$.
In particular the Riemannian measure of $K\cdot x$ is proportional to this quantity. We choose the metric on $\mathbb{X}$ so that we get the desired result.
head: environment

label: rmk: def of Phi
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk: def of Phi}
    It will be convenient to set 
        \[\Phi(v) \coloneqq \prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} (1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha} = e^{-2 \rho(v)} \prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} (2\sinh(\alpha (v)))^{m_\alpha} .\] 
    It is easy from the definitions to read off the bound:
        \[\Phi(v) \leq 1.\]
    The function $\Phi$ is close to $1$ when $v \in \mathfrak{a}^+$ is far from the walls, but tends to $0$ as $v$ gets close to the walls.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the first equivalence. Let $v,v'\in F$ and suppose that $\beta \in (B^N)^*$ satisfies $\beta(v)=1$ but $\beta(v')<1$ then for $\epsilon>0$ small enough, let $\beta_0=\beta-\epsilon\beta'\in F$. We have $\beta(v)>1$ which contradicts the fact that $\beta\in B^N$ and $v \in (B^N)^*$. 
We conclude that $\beta(v)=1$ is equivalent to $\beta'(v)=1$ for $v\in B^N$.

\medskip

We now prove the second characterization. Indeed $\overline{F^\vee}$ is equal to the convex hull of its extreme points, and its extreme points are extreme points of $(B^N)^*$.

label: prop:Bijection vee
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Bijection vee}
    Let $N$ be a polyhedral norm. The map $F\mapsto F^\vee$ is a bijection between the faces of $B^N$ and those of $(B^N)^*$ with inverse $F'\mapsto (F')^\vee$. A face of dimension $p$ of $B^N$ is mapped to a face of codimension $p+1$ of $(B^N)^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the definition, one immediately gets that $\overline{F}\subset \overline{(F^\vee)^\vee}$. For the converse inclusion we just need to check that the codimension of $F^\vee$ is $p+1$ if the dimension of $F$ is $p$. With a similar argument we obtain that the dimension of $(F^\vee)^\vee$ is also $p$.

  \medskip

  For a polyhedral norm, faces $F$ can be written as $\lbrace v\in \mathfrak{a}\mid \forall \omega\in I, \, \omega(v)=1;\; \forall \omega\in J, \omega(v)\leq 1\rbrace$ where $I\cup J$ is a partition of $\operatorname{vert}((B^N)^*)$. Moreover one has $I=\operatorname{vert}(F^\vee)$. Hence, the dimension of $F$ is equal to the codimension of the span of $\omega\in \operatorname{vert}(F^\vee)$, which is equal to the codimension of $F^\vee$ minus one.
head: environment

label: rem:smoothsquare norm
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:smoothsquare norm}
    For general norms on vector spaces, $(F^\vee)^\vee$ may have larger dimension than $F^\vee$, see Figure \ref{fig:smoothsquare norm}. These raises technical difficulties in the general case. This is part of the reason why we restrict ourselves to polyhedral norms.

label: def: standard horofunction
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def: standard horofunction}
    Let $F$ be a face of $B^N$ and let $f \in F$ be any point (recall that, by convention, $F$ is open in its affine span). 
    The \emph{standard horofunction associated to $F$} is
        \[h_F(x) = \lim_{t \to \infty} N(tf-x) -t .\]
head: environment

label: prop:Formula horofunction standard
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Here we use \eqref{eqn: norm from the dual ball} to write $h_F(x)$ as the limit for $t\to \infty$ of:
$$\max_{\beta\in (B^N)^*}\beta(tf-x)-t.$$
For each $t>0$ let $\beta_t\in (B^N)^*$ be a linear form at which the maximum is reached. Let $f\in F$. Then for all $\beta\in F^\vee$ :
$$ t(\beta_t(f)-1)-\beta_t(x)=\beta_t(tf-x)-t\geq \beta(tf-x)-t=-\beta(x). $$
Since $\beta_t(x)$ is bounded by $N(x)$ and $(\beta_t(\tau)-1)\leq 0$, then $\beta_t(\tau)=1-o(t)$. Therefore if we chose $\beta_\infty$ to be any limit point of $(\beta_t)$, $\beta_\infty(f)=1$ and $h_F(x)=-\beta_\infty(x)$. Note moreover that for any $\beta\in F$ we have $h_F(x)\geq -\beta(x)$. Hence $h_F(x)=\max_{\beta\in \overline{F^\vee}} -\beta(x)$.

label: defn:Lin and Lin_0
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:Lin and Lin_0}

Let $\operatorname{Span}(F)$ denote the linear span, i.e.\ the smallest vector subspace of $\mathfrak{a}$ containing $F$.

Let $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)$ denote the linear part of the affine span of $F$, or equivalently the linear span of differences $f-f'$ for $f,f'\in F$.

\medskip 

Dually we define $\operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)$ as the linear span of $\mathfrak{a}$ containing $F^\vee$ and $\operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)$ the linear part of the affine span of $F^\vee$. For a vector subspace $V\subset \mathfrak{a}$ we write $V^\vee=\lbrace \beta\in \mathfrak{a}^*\mid \forall v\in V,\, \beta(v)=0\rbrace$.
head: environment

label: prop:basic properties Lin
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:basic properties Lin}
Let $F$ be a face of $B^N$, where $N$ is a polyhedral norm. We have $\operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)=(\operatorname{Span}_0(F))^\vee$ and $\operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)=(\operatorname{Span}(F))^\vee$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first prove that in general, for any norm $N$, $\operatorname{Span}(F)\subset \operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)^\vee$. Let $f\in F$ and $\alpha, \beta\in F^\vee$ so that $\alpha-\beta \in \operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)$. By definition of $F^\vee$, $\alpha(f)=\beta(f)=1$ so $(\alpha-\beta)(f)=0$. Hence $f\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)^\vee$, and $\operatorname{Span}(F)\subset\operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)^*$.

Similarly one has for any norm $N$ that $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)\subset \operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)^\vee$. Let $f,g\in F$ so $f-g\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$ and $\alpha\in F^\vee$. By definition of $F^\vee$, $\alpha(f)=\alpha(g)=1$ so $\alpha(f-g)=0$. Hence $f-g\in \operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)^\vee$, and $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)\subset\operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)^\vee$.

\medskip

In order to check the equality, it suffices to compute that the dimensions coincide. As in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:Bijection vee}, if $F$ has dimension $p$, $F^\vee$ has codimension $p+1$, so the dimension of $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)$ and the codimension of $\operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)$ coincide. Similarly the dimension of $\operatorname{Span}(F)$ and the codimension of $\operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)$ coincide.
head: environment

label: lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions}
    Let $F$ be a face of $B^N$ and let $v \in \mathfrak{a}$.
    The standard horofunction $x\mapsto h_F(x)$ coincides on $\mathfrak{a}$ with $x\mapsto h_F(x+v)$, if and only if $v\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$. 
    These two functions differ by a constant function if and only if $a\in \operatorname{Span}(F)$.
    
    \medskip
    
    Let $F,F'$ be two faces of the unit ball for $N$. 
    The difference $h_F-h_{F'}$ of the associated standard horofunctions is bounded on $\mathfrak{a}$ if and only if $F=F'$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f\in F$, we have by Proposition \ref{prop:basic properties Lin}:
$$\operatorname{Span}_0(F)=\operatorname{Span}(F^\vee)^*=\bigcap_{\beta\in F^\vee} \operatorname{Ker}(\beta).$$
Clearly translations in this subspace leave invariant the standard horofunction $h_F$ given by equation \eqref{eq:Formula standard horofunctions}.
Note that $\langle f\rangle \oplus \operatorname{Span}_0(F)=\operatorname{Span}(F)$.
For all $x\in \mathfrak{a}$ one has $h_F(x)-h_F(tf+x)=t$, so translating $h_F$ by an element in $\operatorname{Span}(F)$ only changes the horofunction by a constant.

\medskip

Conversely suppose that translating by $v\in \mathfrak{a}$ changes the horofunction by a constant. Up to translating $v$ by a multiple of $f$ with $f\in F$ we can assume that $h_F(x)=h_F(x+v)$ for all $x\in \mathfrak{a}$. In particular since $h_F(0)=0$, one has $h_F(v)=h_F(-v)=0$ so in particulat by \eqref{eq:Formula standard horofunctions}, for all $\beta \in \overline{F}$, $\beta(v)\leq 0$ and $\beta(-v)\leq 0$ so $\beta(v)=0$ and hence $v\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$.

\medskip 

Now for the second point, note that for $v\in \mathfrak{a}$ and $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $h_{F}(tv)=th_F(v)$, and the same holds for $F'$, hence $h_F(v)-h_{F'}(v)=\frac{1}{t}(h_F(tv)-h_{F'}(tv))$ which converges to $0$ when $t$ goes to $+\infty$, meaning that $h_F=h_{F'}$ if the difference is bounded. If we still have $F\neq F'$ then there is up to exchanging $F$ and $F'$ a $\beta\in F^\vee$ such that $\beta\notin \overline{F'^\vee}$. Since $\beta \in F^\vee$ then $h_F\geq -\beta$, but since $\beta\notin \overline{F'^\vee}$, one can find $v\in \mathfrak{a}$ such that $-\beta(v)> 0$ and $-\beta'(v)< 0$ for all $\beta'\in \overline{F'^\vee}$, meaning that $h_{F'}(v)<-\beta(v)$. Hence $h_{F}\neq h_{F'}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
The set of simple roots whose associated symmetry fixes $F$ (and hence $F^\vee$) will be denoted by $\Theta_F^\text{stable}$. This set decomposes as :
    $$\Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}=\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}}\sqcup \Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}}.$$
    Here $\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}}$ is the set of simple roots $\alpha\in \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}$ such that $\alpha \in \operatorname{Span}_0(F^\vee)$ and $\Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}}$ the set of simple roots $\alpha\in \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}$ with $\alpha^\vee\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$.

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md: For $\beta \in \Theta_F^{flipped}$ and $\alpha \in \Theta_F^{fixed}$ it holds that $\beta^\vee \in \operatorname{Span}_0(F) \subset \operatorname{Span} (F) \subset \ker(\alpha)$. Hence $\beta$ and $\alpha$ are orthogonal.

label: prop:a is span of coroots
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:a is span of coroots}
    The Lie subalgebras $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$ and $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$ are respectively the spans of the co-roots $\alpha^\vee$ associated to $\alpha\in \Theta^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$, repsectively $\alpha\in \Theta^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that for all $\alpha\in \Sigma^+$, $\alpha^\vee \in[\mathfrak{g}_\alpha,\mathfrak{g}_{-\alpha}]$, so the spans are contained in $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$ and $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$ respectively. 

Moreover $[\mathfrak{g}_\alpha,\mathfrak{g}_{-\alpha}]\subset \langle \alpha^\vee \rangle \oplus \mathfrak{m}$. 
In particular, we see that in the expression \eqref{eq:Definition Gfixed flip}, replacing $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$ and $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$ by the respective spans of coroots still gives a Lie subalgebra. 
Hence we have the desired result.

label: lem: tau in ker flipped
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: tau in ker flipped}
    There exists $\tau \in F$ so that \( \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}} = \{ \alpha \in \Delta : \alpha(\tau)=0 \} .\)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Any $\tau \in F$ satisfies $\alpha(\tau)>0$ when $\alpha \in \Delta \setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}$ and $\alpha(\tau)=0$ when $\alpha \in \Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}}$.
    Replace any $\tau \in F$ by its average $\tau'$ by the subgroup of $W$ stabilizing $F$, or equivalently by its average under the Weyl subgroup corresponding to $\Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}}$. 
    Then $\alpha(\tau') = 0$ for all $\alpha \in \Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}}$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: The subgroups $R_F\subset S_F$ are contained in the parabolic subgroup $P_{\Delta\setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}}$ and contain the horospherical subgroup $U_{\Delta\setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $h_F$ as the limit of distance functions along $\gamma_\tau (t) = e^{t \tau}K$, with $\tau$ from Lemma \ref{lem: tau in ker flipped}, normalized to be zero at the basepoint.
    
    We first show that $U_{\Delta\setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}} $ is contained in $R_F$. 
    Note that for any $n \in U_{\Delta\setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}}$, the Riemannian geodesic ray $\gamma = \gamma_\tau$ is strongly asymptotic to its translate $n\cdot \gamma$, because $\alpha(\tau)=0$ for all $\alpha\in\Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}$.
    Being strongly asymptotic means that:
    $$ \left\lvert {d^N(x,n \gamma(t)) - d^N(x,\gamma(t))} \right\rvert \to 0.$$
    Hence the limit of distance functions along $\gamma$ and $n\cdot \gamma$ are equal, and in particular $h_F \circ n = h_F$.

    \medskip
    
    Now let $g$ be an element of $S_F$, and suppose that it does not belong to the parabolic $P_{\Delta\setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}}$. 
    Hence $[\gamma]$ and $[g \gamma]$ are distinct points of $\partial_{vis}\mathbb{X}$. 
    Let $A$ be a maximal flat containing both  $[\gamma]$ and $[g \gamma]$ in its visual boundary, and let $\gamma'(t) = e^{t \tau'}K$ be the geodesic ray in the standard flat asymptotic to $g \gamma$ with $\gamma'(0)=K$.
    Choose $g' \in G$ fixing $[\gamma]$, taking the standard maximal flat to $A$, and satisfying $g' \gamma' = g \gamma$.
    
    Since $g' \gamma \sim \gamma$, their associated horofunctions $h_{g' \gamma}$ and $h_\gamma = h_F$ are at bounded distance.
    In particular $h_{g' \gamma}$ is at bounded distance from $h_{g \gamma} = h_F \circ g = h_F$ since $g \in S_F$. 
    These are translates of the horofunctions $h_{\gamma'}$ and $h_\gamma$ by $g'$, so those are also at bounded distance. 
    But since these correspond to distinct faces, this contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions}.

label: prop:comparing RF and SF to Gflip and Gfix
title: Proposition
head: environment
labels: prop:comparing RF and SF to Gflip and Gfix

title: Proof
body_md:
We again write $h_F$ as the Busemann point associated to $\tau$ from Lemma \ref{lem: tau in ker flipped}, and again take $\gamma_\tau$ the corresponding geodesic ray emanating from the basepoint. 
Then every element $g\in K\cap P_{\Delta\setminus \Theta^{\operatorname{stable}}_F}$ fixes the geodesic ray $\gamma_\tau$, and hence preserves $h_F$.

\medskip

Now thanks to the Cartan decomposition for $G^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$ and $G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$, since the maximal compacts subgroups are in $R_F$ we just need to check that the restricted Cartan subgroup of $G^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$ is in $R_F$ and that no non-trivial element of the restricted Cartan subgroup are in $S_F$.

\medskip

Let $\tau \in \mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$, then it is a combination of co-roots  in $\Theta^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$ by Proposition \ref{prop:a is span of coroots}, hence it belongs to $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)$. 
In particular $h_F\circ e^{\tau}=h_F$ on the model flat by Lemma \ref{lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions}. 
Since $h_F$ is in the horoboundary of the model flat and since $e^\tau$ preserves the model flat, this implies that the horofunctions are equal on the whole symmetric space by Theorem \ref{thm:Comparaison Horofunction Flat and symmetric space HSWW}.

\medskip

Now let $\tau \in \mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$. 
It is a combination of co-roots in $\Theta^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$ by Proposition \ref{prop:a is span of coroots}. 
Lemma \ref{lem:flipping roots orthgonal to fixing roots} implies that $\tau$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{Span}(F)$. Hence by Lemma \ref{lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions} the translated horofunction $h\circ e^\tau$ is to equal up to a constant to $h$ on the model flat, so $e^\tau\notin S_F$.
head: environment

label: lem:Cartan subgroup of stabiliazer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Cartan subgroup of stabiliazer}
    We have $\operatorname{Lie}(R_F) \cap \mathfrak{a} = \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(S_F) \cap \mathfrak{a} = \operatorname{Span}(F)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying Theorem \ref{thm:Comparaison Horofunction Flat and symmetric space HSWW}, the horofunctions $h_F$ and $h_F \circ e^\tau$ for $\tau\in \mathfrak{a}$ are equal if and only they coincide on the model flat. 
    The result then follows from Lemma \ref{lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions}.
head: environment

label: prop:Space horofunctions
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Space horofunctions}
    The $G$-homogeneous space $\mathcal{O}_F$ fibers over the flag manifold $\mathcal{F}_\Theta=G/P_\Theta$ where $\Theta=\Delta\setminus \Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}}$. The fiber at each point is a copy of $\mathbb{X}_F$, where $\mathbb{X}_F$ is the  symmetric space associated to the group $G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F\times e^{V}$. Here $V\subset \mathfrak{a}$ is the orthogonal complement of $\mathfrak{a}^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$ in $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)^\perp$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $\mathcal{O}_F = G/R_F$ with $R_F$ in $P_\Theta$, so $G/R_F$ maps to $G/P_\Theta$.
    The fiber is $P_\Theta/R_F$.

    \medskip

    The parabolic group $P_\Theta$ is generated by  the groups $K\cap P_\Theta$, $U_\Theta$, $G^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F$, $G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F$ and $e^\mathfrak{a}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:comparing RF and SF to Gflip and Gfix} we know that 
    $$ \left(K\cap P_\Theta\right)/\left(R_F\cap K\right), U_\Theta/\left(U_\Theta\cap R_F\right), \text{ and } G^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F/\left(G^{\operatorname{flipped}}_F\cap R_F\right) $$
    are trivial, and that $G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F/\left(G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F\cap R_F\right)=G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F/\left(G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F\cap K\right)$.
    
    We use Lemma \ref{lem:Cartan subgroup of stabiliazer} and again part of Proposition \ref{prop:comparing RF and SF to Gflip and Gfix} to see that $$\langle e^\mathfrak{a}, G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F\rangle/\left(\langle e^\mathfrak{a}, G^{\operatorname{fixed}}_F\rangle\cap R_F\right)=\mathbb{X}_F. $$
    Hence $P_\Theta/R_F$ is naturally identified with $\mathbb{X}_F$.

label: prop:Lie algebra of stabilizer
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The roots in $\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}}$ and $\Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}}$ are orthogonal (Lemma \ref{lem:flipping roots orthgonal to fixing roots}), hence every root in ${\operatorname{Span}}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{stable}})$ belongs to exactly one of ${\operatorname{Span}}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}})$ or ${\operatorname{Span}}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}})$.

label: prop: dN from busemanns
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: dN from busemanns}
    Let $o,x,y \in \mathbb{X}$. 
    Then:
        \[ d^N(x,y) = \max_{i \in I, \xi \in G \cdot [b_{\omega_i}]} \left\lVert {\omega_i} \right\rVert(b_{o,\xi}(x) - b_{o,\xi}(y)) .\]
    In particular by setting $o=x$ or $o=y$ we obtain:
       \[ d^N(x,y) = \max_{i \in I, \xi \in G \cdot [b_{\omega_i}]} -\left\lVert {\omega_i} \right\rVert b_{x,\xi}(y)  = \max_{i \in I, \xi \in G \cdot [b_{\omega_i}]} \left\lVert {\omega_i} \right\rVert b_{y,\xi}(x).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that the expression is independent of $o \in \mathbb{X}$.
    Up to applying an isometry, we may assume that $x=o$ and $y=e^a o$ for $a \in \mathfrak{a}^*$, so that 
        \[ d^N(x,y) = N(\vec{d}(x,y)) = N(\vec{d}(o,e^a\cdot o)) = N(a) .\]
    If $a$ belongs to a face $F$ of $B^N$, then 
        \[ N(a) = \sup \left\{ \omega_i(a) : \omega_i \in vert(F^\vee) \right\} \]
    which is realized by a vertex $\omega_j \in vert(F^\vee)$ since the set of vertices is finite, so 
        \[ \omega_j(a) = \left\lVert {\omega_j} \right\rVert(b_{o,[\omega_j]}(o) - b_{o,[\omega_j]}(e^a \cdot o)) .\]

    For the other bound, note that each $\left\lVert {\omega_i} \right\rVert b_{o,\xi}$ for $\xi \in G \cdot [\omega_i]$ is a horofunction of $d^N$, and hence is $1$-Lipschitz with respect to $d^N$.
head: environment

label: lem:P Theta better description
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:P Theta better description}
For every root $\alpha\in \Sigma$, every $f\in F$,  and every $\omega_i\in vert(F^\vee)$, if $\alpha(f)<0$ then $\langle \omega_i, \alpha\rangle=\omega_i(\alpha^\vee)\leq 0$, where $\alpha^\vee$ is the coroot of $\alpha$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that for a given root $\alpha \in \Sigma$, $\alpha(f)<0$. 
   Since $N$ is a norm that is invariant with respect to the Weyl group, given $f\in F\cap \mathfrak{a}^+$, 
   its reflection
   \[ f-2\alpha (f)\alpha^\vee ,\]
   where $\alpha^\vee$ is the coroot of $\alpha$,
   is still inside the unit ball of $N$. 
   Hence 
   \[ \omega_i(f-2\alpha (f)\alpha^\vee)\leq 1=\omega_i(f).\] 
   Therefore $\alpha(f)\omega_i(\alpha^\vee)\geq 0$. Since $\alpha(f)<0$, $\omega_i(\alpha^\vee)\leq 0$.
head: environment

label: defnprop:Definition E_i^F
title: Definition/Proposition
body_md:
\label{defnprop:Definition E_i^F}
 Let $i\in I_F$ be so that $\omega_i\in vert(F^\vee)$, and  consider $[b_{\omega_i}]\in \partial^{Riem}\mathbb{X}$. 
 Let $E_i^F\subset \partial^{Riem}\mathbb{X}$ be the following set:
 $$E_i^F:=K_\Theta\cdot [b_{\omega_i}]=P_\Theta\cdot [b_{\omega_i}].$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have to show that the two definitions agree.
The compact group $K_\Theta$ intersects every connected component of $P_\Theta$, so 
it suffices to check that the orbits agree locally. 
    
The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{p}_\Theta$ of $P_\Theta$ is the sum of $\mathfrak{g}_0$ plus the sum of all root spaces $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha$ such that $\alpha(f)\geq 0$ for every $f\in F\cap \mathfrak{a}^+$. 
Let $\tau_i \in \mathfrak{a}$ be the vector orthogonal to $\operatorname{Ker}(\omega_i)$ so that $\omega_i(\tau)>0$ and $N(\tau_i)=1$. 
The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{p}_i$ of the stabilizer of $[b_{\omega_i}]$ is the sum of $\mathfrak{g}_0$ plus the sum of all root spaces $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha$ with $\alpha(\tau_i)\leq 0$.
Let us write $\mathfrak{m}_i$ for the sum of all root spaces such that $\alpha(\tau_i)>0$ so that $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{p}_i\oplus \mathfrak{m}_i$.

\medskip

In particular, for every $v\in \mathfrak{p}_\Theta$, we write $v=v_1+v_2$ with $v_1\in \mathfrak{p}_i$ and $v_2\in \mathfrak{m}_i$. 
By Lemma \ref{lem:P Theta better description}  if $\alpha(f)<0$ then $\alpha(\tau_i)\leq0$, hence $v_2$ lies inside the sum of all roots spaces $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha$ such that $\alpha$ vanishes on $F$. 
This sum of root spaces is preserved by the Cartan involution $\theta$ corresponding to $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{k} \oplus \mathfrak{p}$. 
The projection of $v$ to $\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{p_i}\simeq T_{[b_{\omega_i}]}\left(G\cdot [b_{\omega_i}]\right)$ is therefore equal to the projection of $\theta(v)$. 
Hence $T_{[b_{\omega_i}]}\left(P_\Theta\cdot [b_{\omega_i}]\right)=T_{[b_{\omega_i}]}\left(K_\Theta\cdot [b_{\omega_i}]\right)$. 
This is sufficient to see that the corresponding homogeneous spaces coincide.
head: environment

label: prop:Explicit formula for Horofunctions
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f\in F\cap \mathfrak{a}^+$. Let $[f]\in \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} \mathbb{X}$ be the class of the ray from $o$ with initial derivative $f$. By definition, $h$ is equal to the following limit, where $f\in F$:
$$h(x)=\lim_{t\to +\infty}d^N(x, exp_o(tf ))-d^N(o,exp_o(tf));$$
$$h(x)=\lim_{t\to +\infty}\max_{i\in I, \, p\in G\cdot [\omega_i]}\lVert \omega_i \rVert \left(b_{p,o}(x)-b_{p,o}(exp_o(f t))\right)-tN(f).$$

Recall that $N(f)=1$ since $f\in F$ is in a face the unit ball of $N$. We individually consider the functions $\phi_{i,p}(t)=-\lVert \omega_i \rVert b_{p,o}(exp_o(tf))-t$ for $i\in I_F$ and $p\in G\cdot [\omega_i]$. These functions are negative and decreasing: indeed $\lVert\omega_i\rVert b_{p,o}$ is $1$-Lipschitz for $d^N$ by Proposition \ref{prop: dN from busemanns}. Hence their limits are well defined in $\mathbb{R}\cup \lbrace -\infty\rbrace$.

\medskip

Morally we are now trying to prove that for this term to appear in the maximum in the limit, we need $[p]$ to be in the $E_i$ previously defined. Else we show that this function converges to $-\infty$ and hence cannot count in the maximum.

\medskip

Let $p\in G\cdot [\omega_i]$ for some $i\in I$. Let $P_\Theta$ be the same parabolic subgroup as before. We can find $g\in P_\Theta$ such that $g\cdot p=p_0\in \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} \mathfrak{a}^+\subset \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} \mathbb{X}$. Let $\pi_0\in \mathfrak{a}^+$ be the vector of unit norm for $N$ corresponding to $p_0\in \partial_{\mathrm{vis}}\mathfrak{a}^+$.  The function $\phi_{i,t}=-\lVert \omega_i\rVert b_{p_{0},g\cdot o}(exp_o(t\pi_0))-t$ is equal up to a constant to:
$$\widetilde{\phi}_{i,p}(t)=-\lVert \omega_i\rVert b_{p_{0},o}(exp_o(t\pi_0))-t=\omega_i(t\pi_0)-t$$ 
Here the constant bounding the difference depends only on the distance between $o$ and $g\cdot o$. 

The function $\phi_{i,p}$ converges uniformly to $-\infty$ away from the set of points $p_0$ such that the associated points satisfy $\pi_0=\tau_i$, where $\tau_i$ as previously is the vector of norm one for $N$ orthogonal to $\operatorname{Ker}(\omega_i)$ with $\omega_i(\tau_i)>0$. This property  $\pi_0=\tau_i$ occurs excatly when $i\in I_F$ and $p\in E^F_i$

\medskip

We write :
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq: formula horofunction inside the proof}
h(x)=\lim_{t\to +\infty}\max_{i\in I, \, p\in G\cdot [\omega_i]} \left( \lVert \omega_i \rVert b_{p,o}(x)+\phi_{i,p}(t)\right).\end{equation}

Let $(i_t)_{t\geq 0}$ and $(p_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be elements of $I$ and $p_t\in G\cdot [\omega_t]$ respectively such that the maximum in \eqref{eq: formula horofunction inside the proof} is reached for this value of $t\geq 0$. Up to taking a subsequence, one can assume that $i_t=i'$ for $t$ large enough, since $I$ is finite.

\medskip
Since $h(x)\neq -\infty$, we obtain that $i'\in I_F$ and $p_\infty\in E_{i'}^F=P_\Theta\cdot [\omega_{i'}]$ so that $\widetilde{\phi}_{i_t,p_t}(t)$ does not diverge to $-\infty$, as previously .

As a consequence we obtain, as in \ref{prop:Formula horofunction standard}: 

$$h(x)=\max_{i\in I_F, \, p\in E^F_i} \left( \lVert \omega_i \rVert b_{p,o}(x)+\lim_{t\to +\infty}\phi_{i,p}(t)\right).$$

By Proposition \ref{defnprop:Definition E_i^F}, if $p\in P_\Theta\cdot [\omega]$ then $p\in E_i^F=K_\Theta\cdot [\omega_i]$. Hence we can assume that $g\in K_\Theta$, and therefore $g\cdot o=o$ which implies $\phi_{i,p}=\widetilde{\phi}_{i,p}$.

title: Remark
body_md: A consequence of the previous proposition is that in the formula for $d^N$ only the Riemannian Busemann functions for directions ``near'' the ray extending $xy$ need to be considered.

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $x,y \in \mathbb{X}$.
    If the segment $xy$ meets a face $F$ of the unit ball in a maximal flat containing $xy$, then 
        \[ d^N(x,y) = \max_{ \omega_i \in vert(F^\vee), p \in E_i^F} \left\lVert {\omega_i} \right\rVert (b_{o,p}(x) - b_{o,p}(y)).\]

body_md: The conventions for labelling the faces are opposite to that of Section \ref{sec:Selberg} for a good reason: the Selberg invariant is close to the metric $d_{\iota\omega_1}$ and not $d_{\omega_1}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: We say that two horofunctions $h_1,h_2\in \mathcal{O}_F$ are in \emph{generic position} if the corresponding flags $f_1,f_2\in \mathcal{F}_\Theta$ are in generic position, i.e.\  their relative position in $W_\Theta\backslash W/W_\Theta$ is the maximal one for the Bruhat order.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
We say that $\mathcal{O}_F$ has the \emph{proper-on-bisector property} if the model horofunction $h_F$ on $\mathfrak{a}$ is proper and bounded from below on the following bisector:
    $$\lbrace v \in \mathfrak{a}\mid h_F(v)=h_F(w_0(v))\rbrace.$$
head: environment

label: prop: proper_on-bisector Plus
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: proper_on-bisector Plus}
    Equivalently $\mathcal{O}_F$ has the proper-on-bisector property if and only if for no non-zero $v\in \mathfrak{a}$, $h_F(v)\leq 0$ and $h_F(w_0(v))\leq 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We need to show that if such a $v$ exists, then one can find a $v'\in\mathfrak{a}$ such that $h_F(v')=h_F(w_0(v'))\leq0$. Note that for all $f\in F$, $h_F(f)<h_F(w_0(f))$ and $h_F(f)<0$. Hence one can find such a $v'$ in the union of two segments in $\mathfrak{a}$: $[f,v]\cup [v, w_0f]$ such that $h_F(v')=h_F(w_0(v'))$, and automatically $h_F(v')\leq 0$ if $v'$ is in the first segment and $h_F(w_0(v'))\leq 0$ if $v'$ is in the second segment.
head: environment

label: prop:MainProp of proper horofunctions
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:MainProp of proper horofunctions}
    If $\mathcal{O}_F$ has the proper-on-bisector property, then for any horofunctions $h_1,h_2\in \mathcal{O}_F$ in generic position, there exist $A,B>0$ such that for all $x\in\operatorname{Bis}(h_1,h_2)$:
    $$h_1(x)=h_2(x)\geq Ad^N(o,x)-B.$$
If $\mathcal{O}_F$ does not have the proper-on-bisector property, then for any pair of horofunctions $h_1,h_2\in \mathcal{O}_F$ in generic position, $h_1$ is not proper and bounded from below on $\operatorname{Bis}(f,g)$.
head: environment

label: lem:Bruhat order
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Bruhat order}
Let $F$ be a face of the unit ball for $B^N$ that intersects $\overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}$. 
Let $x\in \overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}$ and let $w_1,w_2\in W$ such that $w_1\leq w_2$ for the Bruhat order. 
Then $h_F(w_1\cdot x)\leq h_F(w_2\cdot x)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The vertices of $f^\vee$ define linear forms $\omega_i\in \mathfrak{a}^*$ so that  for all $a \in \mathfrak{a}$, $h_F(a) = \max_i \{-\omega_i(a)\}$. 

Each of these functionals is maximized among its Weyl group orbit on $v$, so lies in $W_v \cdot (\mathfrak{a}^*)^+$, where $(\mathfrak{a}^*)^+$ denotes the dominant weights.
By \cite[Lemma 3.4]{KapovichLeebPorti2018dynamicsonflagmanifolds}, it holds that each $\omega_i \in (\mathfrak{a}^*)^+$ satisfies $\omega_i( w_1 x) \ge \omega_i(w_2 x)$. 
Since the set $\{\omega_i\}$ is preserved by $W_v$, this concludes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by proving that the proper-on-bisector property implies that generic pairs of horofunctions are proper on their bisectors.

Suppose that there exists a diverging sequence $(x_n)$ in $\mathbb{X}$ such that $h_1(x_n)=h_2(x_n)$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and $h_1(x_n)/d^N(o,x_n)$ converges to $\ell\leq 0$. Both $h_1$ and $h_2$ are convex for the Riemannian metric as a maximum of Riemannian Busemann funcctions (see Proposition \ref{prop:Explicit formula for Horofunctions}). Up to taking a subsequence, we can assume that the Riemannian segments $[o,x_n]$ converge to a Riemannian geodesic ray $\gamma:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to \mathbb{X}$. We have in particular that $h_1(\gamma(t))\leq h_1(o)$ and $h_2(\gamma(t))\leq h_2(o)$ for all $t\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. 


Let $c^o_1,c^o_2$ be the flags associated to $h_1,h_2$.
Since they are in generic position, there exist opposite
full flags $c_1,c_2\in\mathcal{F}_\Delta$ projecting to
$c^o_1,c^o_2$, respectively.
Choose a Weyl chamber $c$ at infinity containing
$\xi=\gamma(\infty)$, and let
$u\in\overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}$ be the unit vector
representing the type of $\xi$.
Write
\[
w_i=\operatorname{pos}(c_i,c)\in W
\qquad(i=1,2).
\]

We claim that
\[
h_i(\gamma(t))=t\,h_F(w_i u)+O(1).
\]
Indeed, choose a maximal flat whose boundary contains
$c_i$ and $c$.
A ray defining $h_i$, chosen with the type supplied by
Lemma \ref{lem: tau in ker flipped}, and the ray $\gamma$
can both be replaced by asymptotic rays in this flat.
These replacements change the relevant function values
by uniformly bounded quantities.
In coordinates identifying $c_i$ with the model chamber,
the resulting horofunction is a translate of $h_F$,
and the direction of the second ray is $w_i u$.
The claim follows from the fact that $h_F$ is positive homogeneous and Lipschitz.

Since both $h_i$ are bounded above along $\gamma$, we have
\[
h_F(w_1u)\leq0,\qquad h_F(w_2u)\leq0.
\]
Proposition \ref{prop:Tits angle}, applied to the opposite
full flags $c_1,c_2$ and the flag $c$, gives
\[
w_0w_1\leq w_2.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:Bruhat order},
\[
h_F(w_0w_1u)\leq h_F(w_2u)\leq0.
\]
Thus the nonzero vector $v=w_1u$ satisfies
$h_F(v)\leq0$ and $h_F(w_0v)\leq0$, contradicting
Proposition \ref{prop: proper_on-bisector Plus}.


\medskip

Now suppose that the proper-on-bisector property is not satisfied.  Take $(h_1,h_2)$ a generic pair of horofunctions. They can be both seen as a limit of renormalized distance functions along geodesics. Up to acting by $G$ we can suppose that these geodesic are at bounded distance from the model flat and hence up to acting by this element of $G$,  $h_1=h_F$ and $h_2$ is at distance from $h_F\cdot w_0$ uniformly bounded by some $A>0$. In the model flat, the failure of the proper-on-bisector property guarantees that there is a $v\in \mathfrak{a}$ such that $h_F(v)\leq 0$ and $h_F(w_0\cdot v)\leq 0$. The difficulty that remains is that the bisector $\operatorname{Bis}(h_1,h_2)$ is not necessarily at bounded distance from the bisector  $\operatorname{Bis}(h_F,h_F\circ w_0)$.


To circumvent this difficulty we find other poins on the bisector. If $f\in F$, $h_F(w_0(f))-h_F(f)> 0$ since $w_0(f)\notin \overline{F}$. In particular for $r$ large enough $h_1(rf)<h_2(rf)$ and $h_1(rw_0f)>h_2(rw_0f)$. In particular there is an element $x$ in the union of two segments: $[rf,rv]\cup [rv,rw_0f]\subset \mathfrak{a}$ on the bisector $\operatorname{Bis}(h_1,h_2)$. But $h_F(v)\leq 0$ and $h_F(w_0\cdot v)\leq 0$ and $h_F(f)<0$. Hence the element $x$ satisfies $h_F(x)\leq 0$ or $h_F(w_0\cdot x)\leq 0$ which implies that $h_1(x)=h_2(x)\leq A$. When $r$ goes to $+\infty$ the segments in which $x$ lie uniformly go to $+\infty$ so we can find a diverging sequence of such points in the bisector. Hence $h_1$ is not proper and bounded from below on the bisector.

label: prop: proper bisectors
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that we don't have the proper-on-bisector property, so that for some non zero $v\in \mathfrak{a}$, $-\omega_i(v)\leq 0$ and $-w_0\omega_i(v)\leq 0$ for all $\omega_i \in \operatorname{vert}(F^\vee)$ by Proposition \ref{prop: proper_on-bisector Plus}.

Then for every $\omega\in \mathfrak{a}^*$ such that $\omega(v)<0$, $\omega$ does not lie in the cone from \eqref{eq:Convex combination}, so cone is not all of $\mathfrak{a}^*$.

\medskip

On the other hand, if \eqref{eq:Convex combination} does not hold, we may consider the non-empty cone
\begin{equation*}
    V_F = \{ v \in \mathfrak{a} : \forall \beta \in \operatorname{Cone}( F^\vee \cup w_0\cdot F^\vee ), \beta(v) \ge 0\} .
\end{equation*}
Observe that $V_F$ is a convex cone and preserved by $w_0$. 
If $w_0$ is $-\mathrm{Id}$ on $V_F$ then $V_F$ is a vector subspace of $\mathfrak{a}$ where $h_F$ and $h_{w_0 F}$ are identically zero. 
Otherwise, there is $v \in V_F$ with $w=v+ w_0 v$ nonzero. 
Then $h_F( t w) = h_{w_0 F}(t w) \le 0 $ for all $t \ge 0$.
In either case, $h_F$ cannot be proper and bounded below on the bisector.

label: prop:Caracterisation proper bisectors Frho
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h_{F_\rho}$ be a standard horofunction. Its restriction to $\mathfrak{a}$ can be written as the maximum of finitely many functionals $\omega_i$, for $i\in I_{F_\rho}$.
If $ w_0\cdot \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\cap \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\neq\lbrace 0\rbrace$, then the linear span of ${F_\rho}^\vee$ and $w_0\cdot {F_\rho}^\vee$ is not equal to $\mathfrak{a}^*$, and hence \eqref{eq:Convex combination} is not satisfied.

Conversely, by definition of $F_\rho$, $\rho$ is in the interior of $F_\rho^\vee$. 
Then also $-\rho = w_0 \rho$ is in the interior of $w_0 F_\rho^\vee$. 
It follows that $\rho$ is in the relative interior of the convex hull of $F_\rho^\vee$ and $2\rho + w_0 F_\rho^\vee$.
When $ \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho) \cap \operatorname{Span}_0(w_0 F_\rho) = \{0\}$, it holds that the span of $F_\rho^\vee \cup w_0 F_\rho^\vee$ is $\mathfrak{a}^\ast$. 
It follows that the origin lies in the interior of the convex hull of $F_\rho$ and $w_0 F_\rho$, so we may apply Proposition \ref{prop: proper bisectors} to see that $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ has the proper-on-bisector property.

title: Remark
body_md:

    For example, take Figure \ref{fig:A3 example} with the roles of $B^N$ and $(B^N)^\ast$ exchanged. 
    Then the affine span is one-dimensional, but this intersection is zero, and the convex cone is still contained in a proper half-space.

title: Corollary

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $P$ be any polyhedron in $\mathfrak{a}^+\cap \lbrace \rho=1\rbrace $. 
There exist a polyhedral norm $N$ that is Weyl group invariant on $\mathfrak{a}$ such that $F_\rho$ is the relative interior of $P$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us fix a finite family of linear forms $(\omega_i)_{i\in I_0}$ such that $\omega_i\leq 1$ on $P$ and $P\cap \lbrace \rho=1\rbrace=\lbrace x\in \mathfrak{a}\mid \rho(x)=1,\, \forall I\in I_0,\, \omega_i(x)\leq 1\rbrace$. 
 We moreover assume that one of these linear forms is $\rho$. 

We define the norm $N_t$ for all $0\leq t<1$ to be equal for $x\in \mathfrak{a}$ to:
$$N_t(x)=\max_{i\in I_0,w\in W} (1-t)\omega_i(w\cdot x)+t\rho(w\cdot x).$$

For all $0\leq t<1$, $N(x)\geq 1$ for $x\in P_0$. Note that for all $x\in \mathfrak{a}$, and $w\in W$, $\rho(x)\geq \rho(w\cdot x)$ with equality if and only if $x=w\cdot x$. For $t$ close enough to $1$, for $x$ in a neighborhood of $\mathfrak{a}^+\cap P_0$ one has $N_t(x)=\max_{i\in I_0}(1-t)\omega_i(x)+t\rho(x)$. Hence for this norm $F_\rho=P_0$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
It can happen that $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ has the proper-on-bisector property while $F_\rho$ is not a vertex when the opposition involution is non-trivial. 

    In the $D_3 \simeq A_3$ root system, i.e.\ $\mathbb{R}^3$ with 
        \[ \Delta = \{ (1,-1,0),(0,1,-1),(0,1,1)\} \]
    and $\rho$ is (a multiple of) the sum of fundamental weights $(2,1,0)$, take $\omega = (2,2,1)$, see Figure \ref{fig:A3 example}.
    Then the face $F_\rho$ of $B^{N_\omega}$ is an edge joining two rescaled fundamental coweights. 
    The dual ball $(B^N)^\ast$ is a truncated simplex, and one checks that the origin lies in the interior of $\operatorname{Cone}(F_\rho^\vee \cup w_0 F_\rho^\vee)$.
    Hence $F_\rho$ is not a vertex and $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ has the proper-on-bisector property. 

    Notice also that $F_\rho \cup w_0 F_\rho$ spans $\mathfrak{a}$, but generates a convex cone in a proper half-space. 
    So the dual face of the dual norm does not have the proper-on-bisector property.

label: prop:Proper bisectors polyhedral dominant
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Proper bisectors polyhedral dominant}
Let $N=N_\omega$ with $\omega$ dominant and let $F_\rho$ be the face of $B^{N_\omega}$ maximizing $\rho$. Let $\Theta\subset \Delta$ be the set of indices $i$ such that 
$\omega(\tau_i) =\min_{j\in \Delta}\omega(\tau_j)=c$. Then $F_\rho$ is the convex hull of the $\frac{1}{\omega(\tau_i)}\tau_i= \frac{\varpi_i^\vee}{\omega(\varpi_i^\vee)}$ for $i\in \Theta$, or in other words:
$$F_\rho=\operatorname{Cone}(\tau_i,\, i\in \Theta) \cap \lbrace a\mid \rho(a)=\frac{1}{c}\rbrace,$$
$$F_\rho=\operatorname{Cone}(\tau_i,\, i\in \Theta) \cap \lbrace a\mid \omega(a)=1\rbrace.$$
In particular  $\dim(F_\rho)= \#\Theta-1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\omega$ is dominant, any $a \in \mathfrak{a}^+$ satisfies 
        \[ N_\omega(a) = \max_{w\in W} \omega(w a) = \omega(a).\]
    In particular, for each $i \in \Delta$, 
        \[ \frac{\varpi_i^\vee}{\omega(\varpi_i^\vee)} \in \partial B^N = \left\{a \in \mathfrak{a} : N_\omega(a)=1 \right\} .\]

         Moreover, the intersection of $\partial B^N$ with $\mathfrak{a}^+$ is precisely the convex hull of these rescaled fundamental coweights
    \[ \frac{\varpi_i^\vee}{\langle \omega, \varpi_i \rangle}, i \in \Delta. \]

    The face $F_\rho$ is contained in $\mathfrak{a}^+$ since $\rho(w a)$ is uniquely maximized (as $w$ ranges over $W$), on the singleton $W \cdot a \cap \mathfrak{a}^+$. 
    In particular, the closure of $F_\rho$ is the convex hull of 
        \[ \left\{ \frac{\varpi_i^\vee}{\omega(\varpi_i^\vee)} : \frac{\rho(\varpi_i^\vee)}{\omega(\varpi_i^\vee)} \text{ is maximized among } i \in \Delta \right\} .\] 

Note that the inverse of $\frac{\rho(\varpi_i^\vee)}{\omega(\varpi_i^\vee)}$ is precisely $\omega(\tau_i)$, and that $\frac{1}{\omega(\tau_i)}\tau_i=\frac{\varpi_i^\vee}{\omega(\varpi_i^\vee)}$.

label: thm:Empty Interior
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Empty Interior}
Suppose that $G$ is semi-simple.
    Let $h_1,h_2 \in \mathcal{O}_F$ be horofunctions in generic position.
    The set $\operatorname{Bis}(h_1,h_2) \subset \mathbb{X}$ has empty interior.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: If $h_1=h_2$ on a neighborhood of $x_0\in \mathbb{X}$, $M(h^{\ell_0}_1,x)=M(h^{\ell_0}_2,x)$ for all $x$ close enough to $x_0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is a point $p\in M(h^{\ell_0}_1,x)\setminus M(h^{\ell_0}_2,x)$. 
Let $\gamma\colon \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to \mathbb{X}$ be the geodesic ray with Riemannian speed one starting from $x_0$ going in the direction opposite to $p$.
Since Riemannian Busemann functions have unit gradient, we have that $b_{p,o}(\gamma(t))=b_{p,o}(o)+t$ but for all $q\neq p$ in $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} \mathbb{X}$,  $b_{q,o}(\gamma(t))\leq b_{q,o}(o)+(1-\epsilon) t$ with $\epsilon>0$ depending continuously on $q$. 

In particular since $p\in M^1$, $h_1(\gamma(t))=h_1(x_0)+C_{\ell_0}t$ and $h_2(\gamma(t))<h_1(o)-C_{\ell_0}\epsilon t$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Hence if $h_1$ and $h_2$ coincide on a neighborhhod of $o$,  $M(h^{\ell_0}_1x)\subset M(h^{\ell_0}_2,x)$. 

\medskip

For the converse inclusion, we obtain simillarly $M(h^{\ell_0'}_2,x)\subset M(h^{\ell_0'}_1,x)$ where $\ell_0'$ is the smallest index such that $M(h^{\ell_0'}_2,x_0)\neq \emptyset$. As a consequence of the txo inclusions $\ell_0=\ell_0'$ and we have the desired equality.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: If $h_1=h_2$ on a neighborhood of $x_0\in \mathbb{X}$, then, for any small enough neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$, the sets $\bigcup_{x\in  U} M(h^{\ell_0}_1,x)$ and $ \bigcup_{x\in  U} M(h^{\ell_0}_1,x)$  are open subsets of $\bigcup_{i\in I_F}E^1_i$ and $\bigcup_{i\in I_F} E^2_i$ respectively.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The stabilizer $R_F$ of the horofunction $h_1$ contains $K_\Theta$ which acts transitively on $E^1_i$ by the Definition/Proposition \ref{defnprop:Definition E_i^F} and hence also locally transitively on  $E_i$, for all $i\in I_F$. Hence let $p\in E_i$ be close enough to $p_0\in M^1(o)$, then there exist $g\in R$ such that $g\cdot o\in U$ and $g\cdot p_0=p$. (Note that $K_\Theta$ preserves $o_1$ but not necessarily $o$.) Since $g\cdot h_1=h_1$ we also have $M(h_1^{\ell_0},g\cdot o)=g\cdot M(h_1^{\ell_0},o)$. 

We conclude by applying the same argument to $h_2$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be a semisimple Lie group, let $P$ be a parabolic subgroup, and let $w_0$ be a lift of the longest element of the Weyl group.
    Then $P$ and $w_0 P w_0^{-1}$ do not share an orbit in $G/P$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $\zeta^+ \in \partial_{vis} \mathbb{X}$ so that $P$ is the stabilizer of $\zeta^+$. 
    Then $\zeta^+$ is in every orbit closure: $\zeta^+ \in \overline{P\cdot \zeta}$ for any $\zeta \in G \cdot \zeta^+$, and similarly $w_0 \zeta^+ \in \overline{w_0Pw_0^{-1}\cdot \zeta}$ for any $\zeta \in G \cdot \zeta^+$.
    Now suppose for the sake of contradiction that $\zeta$ in $G \cdot \zeta^+$ satisfies $P \cdot \zeta = w_0 P w_0^{-1} \cdot \zeta$. 
    By definition, the Bruhat order corresponds to inclusions of Schubert varieties, i.e.\ closures of orbits of $P$. 
    From 
        \[ \overline{P \cdot \zeta} = \overline{P \cdot \overline{P \cdot \zeta}} = \overline{P \cdot \overline{w_0 P w_0^{-1} \cdot \zeta}} \supset \overline{P \cdot w_0 \zeta^+} = G \cdot \zeta^+ \]
    we see that $\overline{P \cdot \zeta} = G \cdot \zeta^+$, but this implies that $\zeta$ is maximal in the Bruhat order, hence is given by $w_0 \zeta^+$. 
    But this point is fixed by $w_0 P w_0^{-1}$, which yields a contradiction.

label: thm: Convergence measure
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: Convergence measure}
    Let $N$ be polyhedral.
    The $1$-parameter family of measures
     $$\mu_t = \frac1{m_t} (\iota_t)_\ast \operatorname{Leb}$$
    converges vaguely on $\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}$ as $t\to \infty$ to a measure $\mu_N$ supported on $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$. 
   
    This measure $\mu_N$ is the unique $G$-invariant measure on $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ such that $\mu_N(C^o_{-\infty,0})=1$. 
    
    Moreover this measure is \emph{$2\rho_{\max}$-homogeneous}, in the sense that for any measurable set $E\subset \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ and real number $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$, $\mu_N(\lambda\cdot E)=e^{\lambda2\rho_{\max}}\mu_N(E)$, where we consider the $\mathbb{R}$ action on the space of horofunctions given by $\lambda\cdot h(x):=h(x)+\lambda$.

body_md:
\label{lem:ConeBallN}
There exists $A>0$ such that for all $v\in C_\rho\cap \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$:
 $$ \rho(v)\leq - A N(v).$$
 Moreover for some $B>0$ the codimension one volume of the intersection  $C_\rho\cap \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp\cap  \lbrace \rho=-t\rbrace$ is at most
 $Bt^{\dim(\mathfrak{a})-1}$ for $t \ge 1$.

label: lemma: volume of balls
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: volume of balls}
    Let $B^N_{\mathbb{X}}(o,t)$ denote a ball of radius $t$ in $(\mathbb{X},d^N)$.
    Then 
        \[ m_t = vol(B^N_{\mathbb{X}}(o,t)) \sim c t^{\dim F_\rho} e^{2 t \rho_{\max}} \]
    where 
        \[ c = \text{Vol}(F_\rho)\int_{v \in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp} e^{2\rho(v)}\1_{C_\rho\cap H_F} (v) {\prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_{F_\rho}^{\operatorname{fixed}})}}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha} \mathrm{d}\operatorname{Leb}(v) .\]
head: environment

label: lem: Indicator function equalities
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: Indicator function equalities}
    There exists $\epsilon >0$, depending only on $N$, so that the following holds:
     Let $v_F$ be the unique intersection point of the affine spaces $F_\rho+\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$ and $\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$. Let $v\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$. Let us write :
     $$ E(v)= \left\lbrace u\in F_\rho+\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho) \mid \rho(v)\leq -\epsilon d^N(u,F_\rho) \right\rbrace. $$ 
     For all pairs $(u,v)\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\times\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$ and all $t\geq 1$ we have:
     $$\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+\cap B^N}(v/t+u+v_F) \leq \1_{C_\rho\cap H_F}(v)\1_{E(v/t)}(u+v_F).$$

     Moreover for almost every $(u,v) \in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\times\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$:
     $$\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+\cap B^{N}}(v/t+u+v_F)\xrightarrow{t\to \infty}\1_{C_\rho\cap H_F}(v)\1_{\overline{F_\rho}}(u+v_F).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us prove the first part of the statement, namely we prove that if $v/t+u+v_F\in \mathfrak{a}^+\cap B^N$, then $v\in C_\rho\cap H_F$ and $u+v_F\in E(v/t)$.

Let us assume that $v/t+u+v_F\in \mathfrak{a}^+\cap B^N$. 
First we see that $v\in C_\rho$. 
Indeed let $\beta\in F^\vee$, so $\beta(v_F)= 1$ since $v_F\in F+\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$, but $\beta(v/t+u+v_F)\leq N(v/t+u+v_F)\leq 1$. Since $u\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$, $\beta(u)=0$ so $\beta(v)\leq 0$. Since this happens for all $\beta\in F^\vee$, then $v\in C_\rho$.

Now since $v/t+u+v_F\in \mathfrak{a}^+$, for all $\alpha \in \Theta_F^\text{fixed}$, $\alpha(u+v_F)=0$ as $u+v_F\in \operatorname{Span}(F)$ so $\alpha(v/t+u+v_F)=\alpha(v/t)\geq 0$. Hence $v\in H_F$.

Since $N$ is convex and piecewise linear, there exists $c>0$ so that $N(u+v_F) - 1 \ge c d(u+v_F, F_\rho)$. 
Let $C$ be the maximum of $N(x)/N(-x)$ for $x$ nonzero, and let $A$ be the constant from Lemma \ref{lem:ConeBallN}.
Then 
    \[ c d(u+v_F,F_\rho) \le N(u+v_F)-1 \le N(-v/t) \le \frac{C}{A} \rho(-v/t) \]
shows that we may take $\epsilon$ to be $cA/C$.

\medskip

Now for the second part note that the intersection of $E(v/t)$ for $t\to +\infty$ is $\overline{F_\rho}$, so we already have that the right hand side is an upper bound on the limsup everywhere. Now assume that $u+v_F\in F_\rho$ and that $v\in C_\rho\cap H_F$.
For every simple root $\alpha \in \Delta\setminus  \Theta_F^\text{fixed}$, we have $\alpha(u+v_F)>0$ and hence $\alpha(v/t+u+v_F)>0$ for $t$ large enough. 
For the other roots $\alpha\in \Theta_F^\text{fixed}$, $\alpha(u+v_F)=0$ but $\alpha(v)\geq 0$ so $\alpha(v/t+u+v_F)\geq 0$ for all $t>0$. As a consequence for $t$ large enough $v/t+u+v_F\in \mathfrak{a}^+$.

Finally let us write $N(v/t+u+v_F)=\max_{\omega\in \operatorname{vert}((B^N)^*)}\omega(v/t+u+v_F)$. 
Note that if $\omega \in \operatorname{vert}((B^N)^*)\setminus \operatorname{vert}(F^\vee)$ then $\omega(u+v_F)< 1$ so for $t$ large enough $\omega(v/t+u+v_F)< 1$. 
For $\omega \in  \operatorname{vert}(F^\vee)$, $\omega(v)\leq 0$ since $v\in C_\rho$ so $\omega(v/t+u+v_F)\leq 1$ for all $t>0$.  As a consequence for $t$ large enough $v/t+u+v_F\in B^N$. This proves that for almost every pair $(u,v)$, meaning that $u\notin \partial F_\rho-v_F$, we have this convergence.

title: Proof
body_md:
First we recall the formula for volume and rescale into the unit ball.
   Recall that $B^N$ denotes the unit ball of $(\mathfrak{a},N)$, and let $B^N_t$ denote the ball of radius $t$ in $(\mathfrak{a},N)$.
        \begin{align*}
            m_t & = \text{vol}(B_{\mathbb{X}}^N(o,t)) \\
                & = \int_{\mathfrak{a}^+} \1_{B^N_t}(x) d \mu_{\mathfrak{a}^+}(x) \\
                & = \int_{\mathfrak{a}^+} \1_{B^N_t}(x) \prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} \left( 2\sinh(\alpha(x)) \right)^{m_\alpha} \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(x) \\ 
                & = \int_{\mathfrak{a}^+}  e^{2\rho(x)} \Phi(x) \1_{B^N_t}(x) \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(x).
        \end{align*} 

    Here we lightened the notation by writing as in Remark \ref{rmk: def of Phi}:
    \[ \Phi(x) = e^{-2\rho(x)}\prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} \left( 2\sinh(\alpha(x)) \right)^{m_\alpha}, \] 
    Recall that $\Phi(x) \le 1$ for $x \in \mathfrak{a}^+$, and $\Phi(x)\to 1$ whenever $\alpha(x)\to +\infty$ for all $\alpha\in \Sigma^+$. 

    In order to study the limit of this function we decompose an element $x$ of $\mathfrak{a}$ as $u_0+v_0$ with $(u_0,v_0)\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\times \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$. We fix the intersection $v_F\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp\cap (F+\operatorname{Span}_0(F))$, so that in particular $\rho(v_F)=\rho_{\max}$ and apply an affine change of variable $(u,v)\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\times \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$ depending on $t$ : $u=u_0/t$, $v=v_0-tv_F$.
    Note that if $u_0\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$, $\rho(u_0)=0$.
    Then 
    \begin{align*}
        m_t & = \int\limits_{\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp} \int\limits_{\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)} e^{2\rho(v_0)}\Phi\left( u_0+v_0 \right)\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+ \cap B_t^N}\left(u_0+v_0\right)  \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(u_0) \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(v_0) \\
        & = t^{\dim F_\rho}\int\int e^{2\rho(t(u+v_F)+v)}\Phi\left( t(u+v_F)+v \right)\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+ \cap B_t^N}\left(v+t(u+v_F)\right)  \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(u) \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(v) \\
        & =e^{2t\rho_{\max}}t^{\dim F_\rho}\int\int e^{2\rho(v)}\Phi\left( t(u+v_F)+v \right)\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+ \cap B_t^N}\left(v+t(u+v_F)\right)  \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(u) \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(v)
    \end{align*}

Now we apply Lemma \ref{lem: Indicator function equalities}.
For $t\geq 1$, if we write $E(v)=\lbrace u\in \mathfrak{a} \mid \rho(v)\leq - \epsilon d(u,F_\rho)\rbrace$ for some $\epsilon>0$ small enough, we obtain : 
$$\Phi\left( v+t(u+v_F) \right)\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+ \cap B_t^N}\left(v+t(u+v_F)\right)\leq \1_{C_\rho\cap H_F}\left(v\right)\1_{E(v)}(u+v_F) .$$

Note that for all $t\geq 1$, $E(v/t)\subset E(v)$. Hence one can apply the dominated convergence theorem to compute the limit of $m_t e^{-2t\rho_{\max}}t^{-\dim F_\rho}$ if the following integral is finite :
\[ \int\int e^{2\rho(v)}\1_{C_\rho\cap H_\rho}\left(v\right)\1_{E_{v}}(u+v_F)  \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(u) \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(v).\]

But this integral decomposes as:

\[ \int e^{2\rho(v)}\1_{C_\rho\cap H_\rho}\left(v\right)\text{vol}(E(v))\mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(v) <+\infty.\]

This integral is finite as $\text{vol}(E(v))$ is polynomial in $-\rho(v)$, as the volume of the $\rho(v)/\rho_{\max}$-neighborhood of $F$ is $F+\operatorname{Span}_0(F)$, and Lemma \ref{lem:ConeBallN} implies that the volume of the level set of $\rho$ in $C_\rho\cap \operatorname{Span}_0(F)^\perp$ also grows polynomially in $-\rho(v)$.

\medskip

Now let us compute the limit. Under the assumption that $u+v_F\in F_\rho$, then the limit of $\alpha(v+t(u+v_F))$ is equal to $+\infty$, for all roots, except the ones that vanish on $F_\rho$, which are exactly the roots in $\operatorname{Span}(\Theta_{F_\rho}^\text{fixed})$ , for which $\alpha(u+v_F)=0$ (recall that $\Theta_{F_\rho}^{\operatorname{flipped}}=\emptyset$).
Using the second part of Lemma \ref{lem: Indicator function equalities} and this remark we obtain that for almost every $(u,v)\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\times \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp\cap H_F$, when $t\to +\infty$:
$$\Phi\left( v+t(u+v_F) \right)\1_{\mathfrak{a}^+ \cap B_t^N}\left(v+t(u+v_F)\right)$$
$$\to \prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_{F_\rho}^{\operatorname{fixed}})}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}\1_{C_\rho\cap H_F}\left(v\right)\1_{F_\rho}(u+v_F).$$

\medskip

The limit of $m_t e^{-2t\rho_{\max}}t^{-\dim F_\rho}$ is then the following integral, using the dominated convergence theorem:
\[ \int\int e^{2\rho(v)}\1_{C_\rho\cap H_\rho}\left(v\right)\1_{F_\rho}(u+v_F) {\prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_{F_\rho}^{\operatorname{fixed}})}}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}\mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(u) \mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}(v) = c .\]

body_md: For all $-\infty<r<R<+\infty$, the sequence $\left(m_{t+R}/m_{t+r}\right)$ converges to $e^{2\rho_{\max}(R-r)}$ by Lemma \ref{lemma: volume of balls}. Therefore, once restricted to $C^o_{r,R}$ and up to scaling the measures by a sequence of real numbers converging to a positive number, the sequence $\frac1{m_t}(\iota_t)_*\operatorname{Leb}$ restricts to a sequence of probability measures on the compact $C^o_{r,R}$. title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: identifying a/Lin0(F)/W_F^fixed with O_F/K}
    For each $F \in Faces(N)$, we have a natural identification 
        \[ \Psi_F \colon (\mathfrak{a}/\operatorname{Span}_0(F))/W_F^{\operatorname{fixed}} \to \mathcal{O}_F /K .\]
    Moreover, these identifications naturally extend $\Psi$ in the following sense:
   If $(v_n,t_n)$ is a sequence in $\mathfrak{a} \times \mathbb{R}$ such that $t_n \to \infty$ and $v_n - t_n f_0$ converges to $v' \in \mathfrak{a}$ for some $f_0 \in F$, then $\Psi([(v_n,t_n)])$ converges to $\Psi_F([v'])$ in $\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the distance-like functions on $\mathfrak{a}$ associated to $(v_n,t_n)$:
    \begin{align*}
        \iota_{t_n}(v_n)(x) & = N(v_n -x) - t_n \\
        & = \max_{\beta \in (B^N)^\ast} \beta(v_n -x) - t_n \\
        & = \max_{\beta \in (B^N)^\ast} \beta( v_n - t_n f_0 -x) + t_n( \beta(f_0) -1)
    \end{align*}
For all $x\in \mathfrak{a}$ in a fixed compact, the term 
$\beta( v_n - t_n f_0 -x)$
stays bounded and the term $t_n(\beta(f_0)-1)$ goes to $-\infty$ except if $\beta \in F^\vee$, in which case this term vanishes. 
Therefore one has for all $n$ large enough: 
\[ \iota_{t_n}(v_n)(x) = \max_{\beta \in \operatorname{vert}(F^\vee)}\beta( v_n - t_n f_0 -x) = h_{F}(-(v_n-t_n f_0 -x)). \]
Then defining $\Psi_F([v'])$ to be the following horofunction 
    \[\Psi_F([v'])( x)\coloneqq h_{F}(x-v').\]
yields the desired continuity result. 

The fact that this map is well-defined on the quotient by $\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$ is a consequence of Lemma \ref{lem:equivalence of translated horofunctions}. The minus sign in the definition of $\Psi$ comes from the minus sign in the definition of the standard horofunctions $h_{F_\rho}$.

label: lem:LittleLemS
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:LittleLemS}
    Recall that $v_F$ is the intersection of $F_\rho+\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$ and $\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$. Let $w\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$ be such that $v_F+w\in \mathfrak{a}^+$. Then $v_F+w\in S$ if and only if $v_F+w\in \overline{F_\rho}$.  If $v_F+w\in F_\rho$ then $v_F+w$ is in the interior of $S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that for all $\beta\in F_\rho^\vee$, $\beta(v_F+w)=1$. Hence one has $v_F+w\in \overline{F_\rho}$ if and only if $v_F+w\in \partial B^N$, which is equivalent to having $v_F+w\in S$. 

If $v_F+w\in F_\rho$, then for all $\beta\in\operatorname{vert}\left((B^N)^*\right)$ with $\beta\notin \operatorname{vert}(\overline{F^\vee})$ then $\beta(v_F+w)<1$. This remains true in a neighborhood of $v_F+w$, so $v_F+w$ is in the interior of $S$.

label: prop: vague limit of measures in flat
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: vague limit of measures in flat}
    Let $\operatorname{Leb}$ denote the pullback of the Lebesgue measure on $\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp$ under the identification $\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp \cong \mathfrak{a}/\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$.
    The measures $\pi_\ast(\nu^o_t)$ converge vaguely to the measure $\mu_N^o$ satisfying: 
        \[ \mathrm{d}\mu_N^o([v]) = \1_{H_{F_\rho}}(v)e^{2\rho(v)} \frac{Vol(F_\rho)}{c} \prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}})}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}\mathrm{d} \operatorname{Leb}([v]).\]
    Here $c$ is the constant from Lemma \ref{lemma: volume of balls}.
    There is a unique $K$-invariant measure $\mu_N$ on $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ satisfying $\mu_N^o(K \cdot A) = \mu_N(K \cdot A)$ for all measurable subsets $A \subset \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$.
    Moreover $\mu_N(C^o_{-\infty,R}/K)= e^{2\rho_{\max}R}$ for all $R \in \mathbb{R}$.
head: environment
labels: prop: vague limit of measures in flat

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that for a pair $[v,s]\in(\mathfrak{a} \times \mathbb{R})/W$ to be in the support of $\mu^o_t$, and hence of $\nu$, we need to have $s=t$. 
The measure $\pi_\ast(\1_{C_\rho}\nu_t^o)$ can be written as $\phi_t(v) d \operatorname{Leb}([v])$ where $\phi_t(v)$ is equal to the following :
$$\frac{1}{m_t}\int_{w_0\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)}\prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+}(2\sinh(\alpha(v+w_0+tv_F)))^{m_\alpha}\1_{S}(v+w_0+tv_F)\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Leb} (w_0).$$

After a change of variable $tw=w_0$ we obtain:
$$ \int_{w\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)}\frac{t^{\dim F_\rho}}{m_t}\prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+}(2\sinh(\alpha(v+t(w+v_F))))^{m_\alpha}\1_{S}(v+t(w+v_F))\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Leb} (w).$$

We want to apply the dominated convergence to this integral, for $v$ fixed, using the estimate of $m_t$ of Lemma \ref{lemma: volume of balls}. First note that for $v$ fixed, $\1_{S}(v+t(w+v_F))\leq \1_{\mathfrak{a}^++B^N}(w+v_F)$ for all $t$ such that $N(-v)\leq t$, where $\mathfrak{a}^++B^N$ is the $1$-neighborhood of $\mathfrak{a}^+$ for $N$. 
Using this plus the control $\Phi\leq 1$ as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: volume of balls} allows us to apply the dominated convergence theorem to the previous integral, for $v$ fixed, as one can bound the integral by:
$$\frac{1}{c}e^{2\rho(v)}\text{Vol}\left((\mathfrak{a}^++B^N)\cap (F+\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\right).$$



Once $v$ is fixed, $\1_{S}(v+t(w+v_F))$ converges for almost all $w\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$ towards $\1_{F_\rho}(w+v_F)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:LittleLemS} 


Hence the previous integral, which depends on a parameter $v \in \mathfrak{a}$, converges to the following expression when $t\to +\infty$ via the dominated convergence theorem, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: volume of balls}:
$$\frac{1}{c}\int_{w\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)} e^{2\rho(v)} {\prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}})}}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Leb} w), $$ 
which can be simplified to:
$$\text{Vol}(F_\rho)\frac{e^{2\rho(v)}}{c}\prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}})}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}.$$


\medskip

Finally we compute the measure of $C_{-\infty,R}^o$, for $R \in \mathbb{R}$, with respect to $\mu_N^o$:


\begin{align*}
    & \frac{1}{c}\int_{v\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp}e^{2\rho(v)}\1_{\lbrace h_{F_\rho}\leq R\rbrace\cap H_{F_\rho}}(v) \text{Vol}(F_\rho) {\prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}})}}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}\mathrm{d}\lambda(v) \\
    = & \frac{e^{2\rho(Rf_0)}}{c}\int_{v\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)^\perp}e^{2\rho(v)}\1_{\lbrace h_{F_\rho}\leq 0\rbrace\cap H_{F_\rho}}(v) \text{Vol}(F_\rho) {\prod_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Span}(\Theta_F^{\operatorname{fixed}})}}(1-e^{-2\alpha(v)})^{m_\alpha}\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}(v) \\
    = & e^{2\rho_{\max}R}.
\end{align*}

title: Proof
body_md:
We already computed the limit of the projected measures $\pi_\ast\nu_t^o$ where $\nu^o_t$ was defined in (\ref{eqn: nuto}). 
To conclude the proof, we first check that $\mu_N^o$ is the limit of the measures $\nu_t^o$, and then we check that the differences $\mu_t^o-\nu_t^o$, which are positive measures, converge to the zero measure, so we have computed the limit of $\mu_t^o$.

\medskip

Let $f$ be a continuous and compactly supported function on $\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K$.
We write $\pi \colon \mathcal{D}(X)/K \to \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}/K$ using the identifications:
    \[ \overline{\mathfrak{a}^+} \times \mathbb{R} \cong  \mathcal{D}(X)/K \text{ and } H_{F_\rho}/\operatorname{Span}_o(F_\rho) \cong  \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}/K.\]
Let $g=|f-f\circ \pi|$, which is a measurable function defined $\nu_t^o$ almost everywhere.

We already proved in Proposition \ref{prop: vague limit of measures in flat} that :

$$\int_{\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K} f\circ\pi\mathrm{d}\nu^o_t = \int_{\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K} f\mathrm{d}(\pi_*\nu^o_t)\to_{t\to +\infty}\int f \mathrm{d}\mu^o_N .$$


We need to prove that:
$$ \int_{\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K} g \mathrm{d}\nu^o_t\to_{t\to +\infty} 0. $$

Fix an $\epsilon >0$ and choose $r,R\in \mathbb{R}$ so that $C^o_{r,R}/K$ contains the supports of $f$ and $f \circ \pi$ in $S \times \mathbb{R}$. 

We find a compact $E_\infty \subset H_{F_\rho}/\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)\cong \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}/K$ such that $\mu_N^o( E_\infty\cap C^o_{-\infty,R}/K)\geq e^{2\rho_{\max}R}-e^{2 \rho_{max}r} - \epsilon$. 
This exists since $\mu^o_N(C^o_{-\infty,R}/K)=e^{2\rho_{\max}R}$ by Proposition \ref{prop: vague limit of measures in flat}. 
Moreover we may suppose that $\mu_N^o(\partial E_\infty)=0$, and also that $r$ is small enough that $e^{2 \rho_{max}r}< \epsilon$. 

Define $E=\pi^{-1}(E_\infty)\cap (\overline{\mathfrak{a}^+} \times \mathbb{R}_+) \cong \mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})/K$, meaning the pre-image of $E_\infty$, restricted to pairs $(v,s)$ with $s\geq 0$.
Note that for each $t \in \mathbb{R}$, the intersection of $E$ with $\overline{\mathfrak{a}^+} \times \{t\}$ is compact, and the intersection is empty for $t<0$.

\medskip

Now we show that the closure $\overline{E}$ of $E$ in $\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}$ is included $E \cup E_\infty$.
For any sequence $(v_n,s_n)$ in $E$, the sequence $[v_n - s_n v_F]$ is in the compact set $E_\infty$, so up to subsequence $[v_n-sv_F]$ converges to some $[v_\infty]\in E_\infty$. 
If $s_n$ converges then $[v_n]$ is bounded in $\mathfrak{a}/\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$, so $(\rho(v_n))$ is bounded, $v_n$ is in $\overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}$. 
Hence $(v_n)$ is bounded in $\mathfrak{a}$ and converges to a point in $E$.
If $s_n$ diverges, it goes to $+\infty$ as $s_n\geq 0$. 
Then by Proposition \ref{prop: identifying a/Lin0(F)/W_F^fixed with O_F/K} (and remark \ref{remark: vF vs f0}) the sequence converges to a point in $E_\infty$. 
Hence $\overline{E}$ is compact in $\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}$. 

\medskip

We split the following integral: 
$$\int_{\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K} g \1_{C^o_{-\infty,R}}\mathrm{d}\nu^o_t\leq \int_{E} g \1_{C^o_{-\infty,R}}\mathrm{d}\nu^o_t+\int_{E^c} g \1_{C^o_{-\infty,R}} \mathrm{d}\nu^o_t .$$

On $E$, one has $g(x)\to 0$ uniformly as $x\to +\infty$, again by Proposition \ref{prop: identifying a/Lin0(F)/W_F^fixed with O_F/K} and by the uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact $\overline{E}$. 

\medskip

Now on $E^c$, we show that $\nu_t^o(E^c\cap C^o_{-\infty,R}\cap S)\leq 3\epsilon $ for $t$ large enough, which controls the previous integral on $E^c$ for $t$ large enough (note  that we use here the fact that the support of $\nu^o_t$ is on $S\cap( \overline{\mathfrak{a}^+}\times \lbrace t\rbrace)$).
We use the inclusion $E^c\cap C^o_{-\infty,R}\cap S\subset \pi^{-1}(C^o_{-\infty,R}/K\setminus E_\infty)$. 
Hence the measure $\nu^o_t(E^c\cap C^o_{-\infty,R})$ is less than $\pi_*\nu^o_t(C^o_{-\infty,R}/K\setminus E_\infty)$. 
For $t$ large enough, this measure is $2\epsilon$-close to $\mu^o_N(C^o_{-\infty,R}/K\setminus E_\infty)$. 
Here we use that $r$ satisfies $e^{2\rho_{\max}r}<\epsilon$. 
By Lemma \ref{lemma: volume of balls} $\nu_t(C^o_{-\infty,R})\leq \epsilon$ for all $t$ large enough. 
Since $C^o_{r,R}$ is compact, the vague convergence of measures from  Proposition \ref{prop: vague limit of measures in flat} show that $\pi_*\nu^o_t(C^o_{r,R}/K\setminus E_\infty)$ converges to $\mu^o_N(C^o_{r,R}/K\setminus E_\infty)\leq \epsilon$ (we have chosen $E_\infty$ so that $\mu^o_N(\partial E_\infty)=0$). 

Finally $\mu^o_N(C^o_{-\infty,R}/K\setminus E_\infty)\leq \epsilon$ by construction of $E_\infty$, which concludes the proof that $\nu_t^o(E^c\cap C^o_{-\infty,R})\leq 3\epsilon $.
Hence the previous integral over $E^c$ is less than $3 \epsilon\sup(g)$ for $t$ large enough. We have this for all $R$ and $\epsilon>0$.

This concludes the proof of the fact that $\nu_t^o$ converges to $\mu_N^o$.

\medskip

Finally we compute for all $R>0$ the limit of $(\mu_t^o-\nu_t^o)(C^o_{-\infty,R})$. By the asymptotic computation of the volume of balls, $\mu_t^o(C^o_{-\infty,R})=\frac{m_{t+R}}{m_t}$ which converges to $e^{2\rho_{\max} R}$. But for all $r\in \mathbb{R}$, the limit of $\nu^o_t(C^o_{r,R})$ is equal to $\mu_N^o(C^o_{r,R})$ so the limit of $\nu^o_t(C^o_{-\infty,R})$ is equal at least to $\mu_N^o(C^o_{-\infty,R})$, which is equal to $e^{2\rho_{\max} R}$ by Proposition \ref{prop: vague limit of measures in flat}. This suffices to prove the vague convergence of $\mu_t^o-\nu_t^o$ to zero as any compact set in $\overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}/K$ is contained in some of these cylinders.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $G/H$ be a  homogeneous space with $H$ having only finitely many connected components. 
    It admits a $G$-invariant non-zero and locally finite measure if and only if for all $h\in H$, the trace of $ad_h$ on $\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{h}$ vanishes, in which case this measure comes from a smooth volume form and is unique up to multiplication by a scalar.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that the condition is satisfied. Pick any volume form $\omega_H$ of $\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{h}\simeq T_H G/H$. For any $g\in G$, define $\omega_{gH}$ to be the pushforward by left multiplication by $g$ of $\omega_H$. 
    When $H$ is connected, $\omega_H$ is $H$-invariant exactly when our assumption on traces holds.
    When $H$ has finitely many connected components $H_i$, $i\in I$, we pick any $h_i\in H_i$ for $i\in I$ and consider the volume form $\sum_{i\in I}h_i\cdot \omega_H$. This volume form is $H$-invariant, and so induces a $G$ invariant measure on $G/H$.
    
\medskip
    Conversely any $G$-invariant measure on $G/H$, together with the $H$-invariant measure on $H$ define a $G$-invariant measure on $G$, which must be the smooth Haar measure up to a scalar.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h_0\in R_F$ be an element, we want to compute the trace of $\text{ad}_h$ on :
$$\mathfrak{g}/\text{Lie}(R_F)=\mathfrak{a}/\operatorname{Span}_0(F) \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Sigma^+ \setminus \text{Span}(\Theta_F^\text{stable})}\mathfrak{g}_{-\alpha} \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \text{Span}(\Theta_F^\text{fixed})}\mathfrak{p}_\alpha.$$
We can write $h_0=h+k$ with $h\in \mathfrak{p}$, $k\in \mathfrak{k}$ since the trace of the adjoint action of elements in $\mathfrak{k}$ on a y invariant subspace of $\mathfrak{g}$ vanishes. Hence we it suffices to study $h$. Moreover up to conjugating $h$, one can assume that $h\in \operatorname{Span}_0(F)$. 
In this case, the action of $\text{ad}_h$ is diagonal in the previous decomposition. 
Recall that $\alpha \in \Theta^{\rm fixed}_F$ if and only if $\operatorname{Span}(F) \subset \ker \alpha$, so
for every $\alpha \in \text{Span}(\Theta_F^\text{fixed})$, one has $\alpha(h)=0$. Hence the trace is equal to :
$$\sum_{\alpha \in \Sigma^+ \setminus \text{Span}(\Theta_F^\text{stable})} m_\alpha\alpha(h)=\sum_{\alpha \in \Sigma^+ \setminus \text{Span}(\Theta_F^\text{flip})} m_{\alpha}\alpha(h).$$

label: cor: O_F_rho has invariant measure
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor: O_F_rho has invariant measure}
    If $F$ is a subface of $F_\rho$, $\mathcal{O}_F\simeq G/R_F$ admits a $G$-invariant measure.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that for a face $F$ of $B^N$, $\Theta_F^{\operatorname{flipped}}$ denotes the set of simple roots $\alpha\in \Delta$ whose co-root $\widehat\alpha$ is in $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)$.
Note that when $\Theta_F^\text{flip}$ is empty, the linear form \eqref{eqn: form on aff(F)} is $2\rho$.

We first show that for a subface $F$ of $F_\rho$, it holds that $\Theta_{F}^{\operatorname{flipped}} = \emptyset$.
Indeed, if there is some simple root $\alpha\in \Delta$ whose co-root $\widehat{\alpha}$ is in $\operatorname{Span}_0(F)\subset \operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)$, then $\rho(\widehat{\alpha})=0$.
This is not possible since $\rho$ lies in the model Weyl chamber in $\mathfrak{a}^*$ by Proposition \ref{prop: rho in terms of fundamental weights}.

\medskip
Now that $\Theta_F^\text{flip}=\emptyset$, one can directly apply Proposition \ref{prop: Existence measure} to conclude.

label: exmp:Existence Invariant Measures
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exmp:Existence Invariant Measures}
If $G=G_1\times G_2$, and $N$ a polyhedral norm on the Cartan subalgebra for $G$ defined as $\max(N_1,N_2)$ for polyhedral norms on the Cartan subalgebras of $G_1,G_2$, then the face $F_\rho^{1}$ maximizing the sum of all positive roots of $G_1$ admits an invariant measure. Indeed $\Sigma^+ \setminus \text{Span}(\Theta_{F_\rho^1}^\text{flip})=\Sigma^+_{G_1}$ and hence the sum \eqref{eqn: form on aff(F)} is maximized on $F_\rho^1$. 


\medskip

    For $G=\operatorname{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $N=N_{\omega_1}$ as in Section \ref{subsec:Symmetric spaces examples}, One can check that all the faces $F_i$, $1\leq i \leq n-1$ satisfy this property, and hence admit $G$-invariant measures. Indeed for $F=F_i$, $\Sigma^+ \setminus \text{Span}(\Theta_F^\text{flip})$ is the sum \eqref{eqn: form on aff(F)} equals a linear form $2\rho_i+\nu$ where $\rho_i$ is the half sum of all positive roots of a copy of $\operatorname{SL}(i,\mathbb{R})$ in $\operatorname{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$, these roots being of the form $\lambda_j-\lambda_{k}$, $1\leq j,k\leq i$, and $\nu$ a sum of roots of the form $\lambda_j-\lambda_{k}$, $1\leq j\leq i<k$. We see that this linear form $2\rho_i+\nu$ is maximized on $F_i$.

label: prop:Mecke
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Mecke}
Let $\Pi$ be a Poisson point process with intensity $\mu$. For every measurable positive function $\phi:\mathcal{S}\times X\to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ on the space of locally finite collections of points:
    $$\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{f\in \Pi}\phi(\Pi,f)\right)=\int \mathbb{E}\left(\phi(\Pi\cup \lbrace f\rbrace,f) \right) \mathrm{d}\mu(f).$$
The bivariate version of this formula states that for every measurable non-negative function $\phi:\mathcal{S}\times X\times X\to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ on the space of locally finite collections of points: 
    $$\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{f \ne g\in \Pi}\phi(\Pi,f,g)\right)=\int \int \mathbb{E}\left(\phi(\Pi\cup \lbrace f, g\rbrace,f,g) \right)d\mu(f) \mathrm{d}\mu(g).$$

label: lem:MeckeApplied
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:MeckeApplied}
    Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a measurable subset of $\mathcal{S}_X \times X \times X$. 
    Let $\Pi$ be a Poisson point process with intensity measure $\mu$ on $X$. 
    Suppose that for $(\mu \times \mu)$-almost all $(f,g) \in X \times X$, one has almost surely that $(\Pi \cup \lbrace f,g\rbrace, f,g) \in \mathcal{M}$. 
    Then almost surely, for all $f \ne g \in \Pi$, $(\Pi,f,g) \in \mathcal{M}$.

title: Proof
