label: prop: Tessellation
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: Tessellation}
    Almost surely $(\mathcal{C}_h)_{h\in \Pi_0}$ is a locally finite tessellation of $\mathbb{X}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any point $o\in \mathbb{X}$ recall that given $R\in \mathbb{R}$, $C^o_{-\infty,R}$ is the set of horofunctions $h\in \overline{\mathcal{D}^N(\mathbb{X})}\supset \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ such that $h(o)\leq R$. We know by Theorem \ref{thm: Convergence measure} that for every $R>0$, $\mu_N(C^o_{-\infty,R})<+\infty$ and that when $R\to +\infty$, $\mu_N(C^o_{-\infty,R})\to +\infty$. For every $R>0$ the random variable $\#\lbrace h\in \Pi_0\mid h(o)\leq R\rbrace$ follows a Poisson law with parameter $\mu_N(C^o_{-\infty,R})$, hence it is almost surely finite, and almost surely it is non zero for $R$ large enough. In particular there exist $h\in \Pi_0$ that minimizes $h(o)$ and hence $o\in \mathcal{C}_h$. t
    This proves that $\mathbb{X}=\bigcup_{h\in \Pi_0}\mathcal{C}_h$.

    \medskip

    The $G$-orbit $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ in the space of horofunction is a fiber bundle over a flag manifold $\mathcal{F}_{\Delta\setminus {\Theta^{\operatorname{fixed}}_{F_\rho}}}$.
    The projection of the measure is $K$-invariant and hence is comparable with the Lebesque measure. In particular almost surely every pair of points in $\Pi_0$ are opposite.
    Hence by Theorem \ref{thm:Empty Interior} almost surely for every $h,h'\in \Pi_0$, the set $\lbrace x\in \mathbb{X} \mid h(x)=h'(x)\rbrace$ has empty interior. In particular almost surely for all $h\neq h'\in \Pi_0$, $\mathcal{C}_h\cap \mathcal{C}_{h'}$ has empty interior.

    \medskip
    
  If we fix a compact $V\subset \mathbb{X}$ it is contained in the ball centered at some $o\in \mathbb{X}$ with radius $R'>0$. Almost surely $o\in \mathcal{C}_h$ for some $h\in \Pi_0$, and also almost surely $\Pi_0\cap C^o_{-\infty,h(o)+2R'+1}$ is finite. for every $h'\in \Pi_0$ with $h'(o)\geq R'+2h(o)+1$, the $1$-Lipschitz property of $h,h'$ implies that for all $x\in V$, $h'(x)\geq  h(x)+1$ so $x\notin \mathcal{C}_{h'}$, proving that the tessellation is locally finite.

label: thm:ProperBissectro dichotomy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ProperBissectro dichotomy}
   Let $F_\rho$ be the face of the unit ball of $N$ whose closure is the maximal points of the linear form $\rho$. 
   Suppose that $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ has the proper-on-bisector property, then almost surely for every pair of opposite horofunctions $f\neq g\in \Pi_N$, the corresponding side in the tessellation is bounded:
   $$\mathcal{C}_f\cap \mathcal{C}_g=\lbrace x\in \mathbb{X}\mid f(x)=g(x),\, \forall h\in \Pi_N,\, h(x)\geq f(x)  \rbrace.$$

   Conversely if $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ does not have the proper-on-bisector property, then almost surely for every pair $f\neq g\in \Pi_N$, the corresponding side in the tessellation is unbounded.

label: lem:Matrix Coefficient Vanishing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Matrix Coefficient Vanishing}
For all $A\subset \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ of finite measure for $\mu_N$, one has $\mu_N(A\cap g_nA)\to 0$ for every diverging sequence $(g_n)$ in $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider the unitary representation $\mathrm{L}^2(\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}, \mu_N)$ of $G$. Decompose $G$ into simple factors $G=G_1\times\cdots \times G_n$, up to taking a finite quotient. Let us first prove that this representation does not admit any $G_i$-invariant vector. The orbit $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}=G/R_{F_\rho}$ projects $G_i$-equivariantly onto $G_i/R_i$ where $R_i$ is the projection onto $G_i$ of $R_{F_\rho}$. Hence the invariant vector can be projected to this homogeneous space, and must be trivial if $R_i$ is included to either a maximal compact subgroup or a parabolic subgroup. Indeed the pushforward of $f^2\mu_N$ would give a finite $G_i$-invariant measure on the symmetric space or a flag manifold. 

We now use Propositon \ref{prop:Lie algebra of stabilizer}. If there is some root of $G_i$ in $\Delta\setminus \Theta_{F_\rho}^\text{stable}$ then $R_i$ belongs to a parabolic subgroup. Else all roots of $G_i$ are in $\Theta^\text{fixed}_{F_\rho}$ ($\Theta^\text{flipped}_{F_\rho}$ is empty) and hence $G_i\subset G^\text{fixed}$, and $R_i$ is in a maximal compact subgroup of $G_i$. 

\medskip

We proved that there is no $G_i$-invariant element in $\mathrm{L}^2(\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}, \mu_N)$. The Lie group $G$ satisfies the hypothesis of \cite[{Theorem 9.1}]{BFGM07}, hence every matrix coefficient goes to zero for any diverging sequence $(g_n)$ in $G$, meaning that for all $f_1,f_2\in \mathrm{L}^2(\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}, \mu_N)$:
$$\int f_1 (f_2\circ g_n^{-1})\mathrm{d}\mu_N\to 0.$$

Applying this to $f_1=f_2=\1_A$ yields the desired result.

label: lem:3 conditions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:3 conditions}
    Let $h_0\in \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ be a horofunction and let $E\subset \mathbb{X}$ be a subset. Let $\mathcal{C}_{h_0}$ be the cell corresponding to $h_0$ in the Voronoi diagam for $\Pi_0\cup \lbrace h_0 \rbrace$, where $\Pi_0\subset \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ is a Poisson point process with measure intensity $\mu_N$.
    \begin{itemize} 
    \item[(i)] Suppose that $h_0$ has linear growth on $E$ , meaning that for some $A,B>0$, for all $x\in E$:
$$h_0(x)\geq Ad^N(o,x)-B.$$

Then almost surely $\mathcal{C}_{h_0}\cap E$ is bounded.

\item[(ii)] Suppose that $E$ is unbounded. If $h_0$ is not proper and bounded from below on $E$, then almost surely $\mathcal{C}_{h_0}\cap E$ is unbounded.

\item[(iii)]  Suppose that $-h_0$ has linear growth on $E$,  meaning that for some $A,B>0$, for all $x\in E$:
$$h_0(x)\leq -Ad^N(o,x)+B.$$

Suppose also that the $1$-neighborhood $E_1$ of $E$ has subexponential volume growth, meaning that the volume of $E_1\cap B(o,t)=o(e^{\epsilon t})$ for all $\epsilon>0$. Then almost surely $E\setminus \mathcal{C}_{h_0}$ is bounded.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first prove the point $(i)$.
    Let $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ be a set of points in $E$ such that every point in $E$ is at distance at most $2$ from some $x_i$, and so that for $i\neq j$, $d(x_i,x_j) \geq 1$. Let $M_i$ be the event that the ball of radius $2$ abound $x_i$ intersects non-trivially $\mathcal{C}_{h_0}$, i.e such that for some $x$ with $d(x,x_i)\leq 2$, for all $h\in \Pi_0$, $h_0(x)\leq h(x)$.
    
    
    The probability of $M_i$ is less than the probability that $\Pi_0$ contains no horofunction $h$ such that $h(x_i)\leq Ad^N(o,x_i)-B-4$. The measure of the set of all such $h\in \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ is equal to at least $e^{A'd(o,x_i)-B'}$ for some $A',B'>0$, using Proposition \ref{prop: vague limit of measures in flat}. Recall that if a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson law with intensity $\lambda$, $\mathbb{P}(X=0)=e^{-\lambda}$. In particular :
$$\mathbb{P}(M_i)\leq e^{-e^{A'd(o,x_i)-B'}}.$$

The number of $i\in I$ such that $d(o,x)\leq n$ is at most $e^{Dn}$ for some $D>0$ since the balls of radius $1$ around the $x_i$ are disjoint, of fixed volume, and the volume of balls in the symmetric space $\mathbb{X}$ is exponential. Therefore:

$$\sum_{i\in I}\mathbb{P}(M_i)\leq \sum_{n\geq 0} e^{Dn}e^{-e^{A'n-B'}}.$$
This sum converges, so by the Borel-Cantelli lemma, almost surely only finitely many of the events $M_i$ occur.

\medskip

We now move to $(ii)$. This part of the proof is very close to the argument in \cite[{Proposition 6.2}]{FMW23poissonvoronoi}. 
We take an infinite diverging sequence $(x_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $E$ such that for some $m>0$ for all $i\in \mathbb{N}$, $h(x_i)< m$, that exists since $h$ is not proper on $E$. 
Let $N_i$ be the event $\Pi_0\cap C^{x_i}_{-\infty,m}=\emptyset$, which implies in particular that $x_i\in \mathcal{C}_{h_0}$.
The probability of the event $N_i$ is equal as previously to $e^{-\mu_N(C^{x_i}_{-\infty,m})}\geq e^{-e^{2\rho_{max}M}}$.

Up to taking a subsequence of the diverging sequence $(x_i)$, and thanks to Lemma \ref{lem:Matrix Coefficient Vanishing}, one can assume that for all $i<j\in \mathbb{N}$:
$$\mu_N(C^{x_i}_{-\infty,m}\cap C^{x_j}_{-\infty,m})\leq \log(1+2^{-i-j}).$$

Hence $\mathbb{P}(N_i\cap N_j)=e^{-\mu_N(C^{x_i}_{-\infty,m}\cup C^{x_j}_{-\infty,m})}\leq \mathbb{P}(N_i)\mathbb{P}(N_j)(1+\frac{1}{2^{i+j}})$. This and the fact that $\mathbb{P}(N_i)\geq \exp(-e^{2\rho_{\max}m})$ allows us to get that the following limit is equal to $1$:

$$\lim_{n\to +\infty}\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}(N_i))^2}{\sum_{i,j=1}^n\mathbb{P}(N_i\cap N_j)}= 1.$$

Using the Kochen-Stone generalisation of the Borel-Cantelli Lemma \cite{KS64}, we obtain that infinitely many of the events $N_i$ occur.

\medskip

 Finally let us prove $(iii)$. We consider as previously a set of points $(x_i)$ and we denote by $\overline{M}_i$ the complementary event to $M_i$, i.e.\  the probability that the ball of radius $2$ abound $x_i$ contains no point $x$ such that $f(x)> h(x)$ for some $h\in \Pi_N$.

 \medskip

 By the definition of the Poisson distribution, as before we have for some $A',B'>0$:
 $$\mathbb{P}(\overline{M}_i)\leq 1-e^{-e^{-A'd(o,x_i)+B'}}\leq e^{-A'd(o,x_i)+B'} $$

 The number of $i\in I$ such that $d(o,x)\leq n$ for $n$ large enough is subexponential by hypothesis since the balls of radius $1$ around the $x_i$ are disjoint. Therefore for some $A'',B''>0$:
$$\sum_{i\in I}\mathbb{P}(\overline{M}_i)\leq \sum_{n\geq 0} e^{-A''n+B''}.$$
This sum converges, so by the Borel-Cantelli lemma, almost surely only finitely many of the events $\overline{M}_i$ occur.

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the Mecke formula (Lemma \ref{lem:MeckeApplied}) the theorem boils down to showing that given two $f,g\in \mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ in generic position, if $\Pi_0$ is a Poisson point process on $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ with measure intensity $\mu_N$ and $(\mathcal{C}_h)_{h\in \lbrace f,g\rbrace\cup \Pi_0}$ is the corresponding Voronoi diagram, the side $ \mathcal{C}_f\cap \mathcal{C}_g$ is bounded or unbounded depending on the behavior of $f$ on it. Note that  $\mathcal{C}_f\cap \mathcal{C}_g=\mathcal{C}_f\cap \operatorname{Bis}(f,g)$. 

\medskip

We use the characterisation of the proper-on-bisector property from Proposition \ref{prop:MainProp of proper horofunctions}. If $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ has the proper-on-bissector property, part (i) of Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditions} implies that almost surely $\operatorname{Bis}(f,g)\cap \mathcal{C}_f$ is bounded, which concludes that the side is bounded. 

If $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ does not have the proper-on-bissector property, part (ii) of Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditions} implies that almost surely $\operatorname{Bis}(f,g)\cap \mathcal{C}_f$ is unbounded. This concludes the proof.

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be symmetric space of non-compact type with a polyhedral Finsler metric associated to a norm $N_\omega=\max_{w\in W}w\cdot \omega$ for a linear form $\omega\in \mathfrak{a}^*$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item 
Let $n$ be the rank of $\mathbb{X}$ and let $(\tau_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$ be the renormalized fundamental co-weights defined in Section \ref{subsection:Tau_i}, that satisfy $\rho(\tau_i)=1$ for all $i$.
If for some $1\leq i\leq n$, $\forall j\neq i,\;\omega(\tau_i)<\omega(\tau_j)$, then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_{N_\omega}$ has bounded sides. 

In particular, if $\mathbb{X}$ is a rank-one symmetric space, the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation has bounded sides. 
    \item 
Let the rank of $\mathbb{X}$ be bigger or equal to two, and let $\omega=\rho$, then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_{N_\rho}$ has unbounded sides. 

\end{enumerate}

title: Proof

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\mathbb{X}=\mathcal{X}_1\times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_d$ be a product of rank one symmetric spaces of non-compact type, with $\mathcal{X}_i$ equipped with the normalized Riemannian distance $d_i$. 
Let us consider for some positive $0<a_1\leq a_2\leq \cdots\leq a_n$ the polyhedral Finsler metric:
    $$d_a((x_i),(y_i))=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i d_i(x_i,y_i).$$
\begin{itemize}
\item[-] If $a_1<a_2$, then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_a$ has bounded sides,
\item[-] If $a_1=a_2$, then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_a$ has unbounded sides.
\end{itemize}
Let us consider for some positive $a_1\geq a_2\geq \cdots\geq a_n>0$ the polyhedral Finsler metric:
    $$d_\infty((x_i),(y_i))=\max(d_i(x_i,y_i)).$$
Then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d$ has bounded sides.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Cartan subalgebra for the associated Lie group $G$ is naturally $\mathbb{R}^n$, and note that the opposition involution is trivial, as the Weyl group is just the group of elements acting like $\operatorname{Diag}(\pm1,\cdots \pm1)$. Note also that $\rho=\rho_1+\cdots +\rho_n$ is the sum of the half sums of roots for the symmetric spaces $\mathcal{X}_i$.

For the metric $d_a$, the face $F_\rho$ has dimension $k$, which is the maximum integer such that $a_1=a_k$. By Corollary \ref{cor: proper bisectors when opposition involution is trivial}, $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ has the proper-on-bisector property if and only if $k=1$, which concludes the proof.

For the metric $d_\infty$, the face $F_\rho$ is the vertex $(1,\cdots, 1)$, which concludes the proof once again by Corollary \ref{cor: proper bisectors when opposition involution is trivial}.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2$ be two symmetric spaces of non-compact type  associated to semi-simple groups $G_1,G_2$ with polyhedral Finsler metrics associated to norms $N_1,N_2$ on their Cartan subalgebras $\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2$. 

Given the norm $N_\infty=\max(N_1,N_2)$ the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_{N_\infty}$ has bounded sides if and only if both the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_{N_1}$ and $d_{N_2}$ have bounded sides.

\medskip

Given the polyhedral norm $N=N_1+N_2$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[-] If $N_1(\rho_1)>N_2(\rho_2)$, then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_N$ has bounded sides if and only if the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_{N_1}$ have bounded sides.
    \item[-] If $N_i(\rho_i)=N_i(\rho_i)$ and both opposition involutions for $G_1,G_2$ are trivial, then the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $d_N$ has unbounded sides.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $N_\infty$, note that $F_\rho$ is naturally $F_{\rho_1}\times F_{\rho_2}$. In particular $\operatorname{Span}_0(F_\rho)=\operatorname{Span}_0(F_{\rho_1})\oplus \operatorname{Span}_0(F_{\rho_2})$. Let $(w_0^1,w_0^2)$ be the opposition involution on $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{a}_1\oplus \mathfrak{a}_2$. The intersection from Proposition \ref{prop:Caracterisation proper bisectors Frho}, that characterizes the proper-on-bisector property for $F_\rho$, is empty if and only if it is empty for $\mathcal{X}_1$ and $\mathcal{X}_2$. This concludes the proof.

\medskip

For $N$, note that $F_\rho$ is equal to $F_{\rho_1}$ in the first case and is equal to $F_{\rho_1}\oplus F_{\rho_2}$ in the second. As before the opposition involution on $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{a}_1\oplus \mathfrak{a}_2$ writes as $(w_0^1,w_0^2)$. Hence in the first case we obtain once again the result by Proposition \ref{prop:Caracterisation proper bisectors Frho}. In the second case $F_{\rho}$ is the affine span of $F_{\rho_1}$ and $F_{\rho_2}$, which is not a vertex, hence giving the desired result by Corollary \ref{cor: proper bisectors when opposition involution is trivial}.

title: Remark
body_md: We believe that this result also holds in the case $N_1(\rho_1)>N_2(\rho_2)$ when the metric $N_2$ is a general Finsler norm that is not polyhedral, for instance for Euclidean metrics. However we do not define the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for such non-polyhedral metrics in this paper.

title: Definition
body_md:
Given two points $X\in \mathcal{X}$ and $Y\in \mathcal{X}^*$, the \emph{Selberg invariant} is equal to :
$$\mathfrak{s}(X,Y)= \frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}(XY).$$ 
Here $X$ is again viewed as a linear map $V\to V^*$ and $Y$ as a linear map $V^*\to V$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $X\in \mathcal{X}$ and $Y\in \mathcal{X}^*$, $\mathfrak{s}(X,Y)\geq 0$ with equality if and only if $Y= X^{-1}$, i.e.\  if $X$ and $Y$ correspond to the same point in $\mathbb{X}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The endomorphsim $XY:V\to V$ has determinant one, it is symmetric with respect to the scalar product defined by $X$ and positive. Hence if we write $\lambda_1,\cdots \lambda_n>0$ for its eigenvalues, one has $\operatorname{Tr}(XY)=\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n$ and $1=\lambda_1\cdots \lambda_n$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(XY)\geq n$ with equality if and only if $X^{-1}=Y$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: When $n=2$, one can identify $\mathbb{X}$ with the hyperbolic plane, and in this case $\mathfrak{s}(x,y) = \frac12 \log \cosh(d(x,y))$.
head: environment

label: prop:Compariason SelbergDistance
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Compariason SelbergDistance}
Given $X\in \mathcal{X}\simeq \mathbb{X}$ and $Y\in \mathcal{X}^*\simeq \mathbb{X}$; $d_{\omega_1}(Y,X)$ is half the logarithm of the largest eigenvalue of $XY:V^*\to V^*$. In particular:
$$d_{\omega_1}(Y,X)-\frac12 \log(n)\leq \mathfrak{s}(X,Y)\leq d_{\omega_1}(Y,X).$$
$$d_{\iota\omega_1}(X,Y)-\frac12 \log(n)\leq \mathfrak{s}(X,Y)\leq d_{\iota\omega_1}(X,Y).$$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In what follows, we want to consider a tessellation of $\mathcal{X}$ with convex tiles, so we want $X\in \mathcal{X}$ to be the first argument. Hence the Finsler metric that will appear will be $d_{\iota\omega_1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recalll that $g\in \operatorname{SL}(V)$ acts on $S^2V$ by $g\cdot X= g Xg^{*}$, where $g^*:V^*\to V^*$ is the dual of $g$, when $X$ is viewed as an element $V^*\to V$. The vector valued distance between $X\in \mathcal{X}$ and $Y\in \mathcal{X}^*$ is the element $(\lambda_1, \cdots, \lambda_n)\in \mathfrak{a}$ such that $\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n$ and the eigenvalues of $XY:V^*\to V^*$ are $(e^{2\lambda_1}, \cdots, e^{2\lambda_n})$. We can rewrite $\mathfrak{s}(X,Y)$ as 
$$\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^ne^{2\lambda_i}\right).$$
From that and the expression of $d_{\omega_1}$ we deduce the result.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: We will also consider the \emph{Satake compactification} $\partial \mathcal{X}$, which is natually a compactification of $\mathcal{X}$, and is the projectivisation of $\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{X}^*)=S^2_{\geq 0} V\setminus S^2_{> 0} V$.

label: prop:Identification Selberg and Finler
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If we fix a model pointed flat, the stabilizer of the model horofunction $h_{F_k}\in \mathcal{O}_{F_k}$, as described in Section \ref{subsec:The stabilizer of a horofunction} is the set of matrices that can be written as:

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}
B & 0 \\
A & U
\end{pmatrix}.$$
Here $(B,U)\in S(\operatorname{GL}(k,\mathbb{R})\times\operatorname{SO}(n-k,\mathbb{R}))$ and $A$ is any $(n-k)\times k$ matrix. This subgroup is equal to the stabilizer of the semi-positive bilinear form $Y_0\in S^2 {V^*}^{\geq 0}\setminus S^2{V^*}^{>0 }$, which is associated to the following symmetric matrix written in block form with blocks of size $(k,n-k)$:
$$Y_0=\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 \\
0 & \mathrm{Id}
\end{pmatrix}.$$
Here we view this matrix as a bilinear from, using the standard scalar product associated with the base-point $o\in \mathcal{X}$.
Hence as homogeneous spaces one can identify $\mathcal{O}_{F_k}=G/R_{F_k}$ with $\mathcal{O}_k$ so that $\phi(h_{F_k})=Y_0$. 


\medskip

Hence one can define a bijection $\phi: \overline{\mathcal{D}^{N_{\iota\omega_1}}(\mathbb{X})}\to S^2(V^*)^{\geq 0}$ 
that identifies for $Y\in \mathbb{X}\simeq \mathcal{X}^{-1}$ and $c\in \mathbb{R}$ the function $d(\cdot,Y)+c$ with $e^{2c}Y$, so that $\mathfrak{s}(\cdot,Y)+c=\mathfrak{s}(\cdot , e^{2c}Y)$. This identifies each $\mathcal{O}_{F_k}$ with $\mathcal{O}_k$ as previously described. This map clearly satisfies $(ii)$ and $(iii)$.

\medskip

In order to check $(i)$, one can use Proposition \ref{prop:Compariason SelbergDistance}, so it only remains to consider the case when $Y\in \mathcal{O}_{F_k}$, $1\leq k\leq n-1$.

The standard horofunction $h_{F_k}\in \mathcal{O}_{F_k}$ has the following formula, given the choice of a basepoint  $X_0\in \mathcal{X}$ and a model flat, by Proposition \ref{prop:Explicit formula for Horofunctions}:
 $$h_{F_k}(X)= \max_{\alpha\in \operatorname{Ker}(Y_0)^*} \frac{1}{2}\log(X(\alpha, \alpha)/X_0(\alpha,\alpha)).$$
 Here $\operatorname{Ker}(Y_0)^*\subset V^*$ is the space of linear forms vanishing on $\operatorname{Ker}(Y_0)\subset V$.

 \medskip

 We write $X$ as a symmetric matrix with the following block form:
 $$X=\begin{pmatrix}
 * & * \\
 * & X'
 \end{pmatrix}.$$

 We obtain that $\mathfrak{s}(X,\phi(h_{F_k}))=\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}(X'{X_0}_{|\operatorname{Ker}(Y_0)^*}))$ and $h_{F_k}(X)$ is half the operator norm of $X'$, for the metric $X_{|\operatorname{Ker}(Y_0)^*}$. The inequality $(i)$ follows directly from that.

 \medskip

 Now let us check that $\phi$ is continuous. This is an adaptation of the arguments of \cite[Theorem 5.5]{haettel2018horofunctioncompactificationssymmetricspaces}. Let $(h_m)_{m\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\overline{\mathcal{D}^{N_{\iota\omega_1}}(\mathbb{X})}$ that converges to $h_\infty \in \mathcal{H}^{N_{\iota\omega_1}}(\mathbb{X})$. We will prove that for any subsequence of $(h_m)$, there is a sub-subsequence that converges to $\phi(h_\infty)$. 
 
 First one can assume that $h_m=d(\cdot,y_m)+t_m$ for some $y_m\in \mathbb{X}$ and $t_m\in \mathbb{R}$, up to replacing $(h_m)$ by a distance functions that is close enough, so that the limit remains unchanged. 

 Now fix $X_0\in \mathcal{X}$ a basepoint in the model flat as previously and write $y_m=k_m\cdot \exp(\iota v_m)\cdot o$ with $v_m\in \mathfrak{a}^+$ in the model Cartan subalgebra. 
 Up to taking a subsequence one can assume that $k_m$ converges to $k_\infty\in K$.
 Let $\mathcal{O}_{F_k}$ be the orbit of the space of horofunctions containing $h_\infty$. 
 This means that $v_m=\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda_1^{(m)},\cdots, \lambda_n^{(m)})\in \mathfrak{a}^+$ is such that 
 $(\lambda_1^{(m)}-t_m,\cdots, \lambda_k^{(m)}-t_m)$ converge to some real numbers 
 $(\lambda_{1}^\infty,\cdots, \lambda_{n-k}^\infty)$ but $\lambda_{k+1}^{(m)}-t_m\to -\infty$. 
 In this case the matrices corresponding to the corresponding points in $S^2{V^*}^{\geq 0}$ are the following, using the base bilinear form $X_0$:
 $$k_m\cdot \operatorname{Diag}(e^{2\lambda_n^{(m)}-t_m}, \cdots, e^{2\lambda_1^{(m)}-t_m}).$$

This converges to $k_\infty \operatorname{Diag}(0,\cdots, ,0,e^{\lambda_{n-k}^\infty},\cdots, e^{\lambda_{1}^\infty})$, which is equal to $\phi(h_\infty)$ since $\phi$ is equivariant and $h_\infty=k_\infty\cdot\exp(\operatorname{Diag}(0,\cdots,0,\lambda_{n-k}^\infty,\cdots, \lambda_1^\infty))\cdot h_{F_k}$. This concludes the proof of the continuity.


 \medskip

 Finally note that $\phi$ is proper. Indeed any compact set in $S^2{V^*}^{\geq 0}$ is contained for some $C>0$ in the set of elements $Y$ such that $-C\leq \mathfrak{s}(X_0,Y)\leq C$. The pre-image of this set is compact by $(ii)$, since the set of horofunctions $h$ such that $-C-\log(n)/2 \leq h(X_0)\leq C+\log(n)/2$ is compact. 
 Hence $\phi$ is a homeomorphism.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the kernels of $Y_1,Y_2$ are disjoint, then $Y_1+Y_2$ is positive, and for some $\epsilon>0$, for all $X\in \mathcal{X}$:
$$\operatorname{Tr}(XY_1)+\operatorname{Tr}(XY_2)\geq \epsilon \operatorname{Tr}(XO).$$

Hence if we assume $\operatorname{Tr}(XY_1)=\operatorname{Tr}(XY_2)$, then :
$$\mathfrak{s}(X,Y_1)\geq 1/2\log(\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}(XO)/2n)\geq \mathfrak{s}(X,O)+\frac{1}{2}\log(\epsilon/2).$$

This concludes the proof.

In particular $\mu_{1}$ is equal to the pushforward by the homeomorphism $\phi$ from Proposition \ref{prop:Identification Selberg and Finler} of the measure $\mu_{N_{\iota \omega_1}}$ on $\mathcal{O}_{F_{1}}=\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ obtained previously from a limiting process, up to a scalar.

title: Proof
body_md:
For all $1\leq k<n$, the face $F_k$ satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition \ref{prop: Existence measure}. 
The measure $\mu_k$ is then the unique invariant measure. In the case $k=1$ it must coincide with the $G$-invariant measure $\mu_{N_{\iota \omega_1}}$.

label: lem: Selberg Control volume cones
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: Selberg Control volume cones}
There exist a constant $\frac{1}{n^{2\rho_{max}}}<C_{1}<n^{{2\rho_{max}}}$ where $2\rho_{\max}=n^2-n$ such that for all $X\in \mathcal{X}$ and $R\in \mathbb{R}$:
$$\mu_{1}(\mathfrak{C}^X_{-\infty,R})=C_{1}e^{2\rho_{\max} R}.$$
The measures $\mu_k$ also satisfy $\mu_{k}(\mathfrak{C}^X_{-\infty,R})=C_ke^{\delta_k R}$ for some $C_k,\delta_k>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us consider the cylinders $C^x_{-\infty,R}$ defined previously as the sets of elements $Y_0$ such that $h_{\phi^{-1}(Y_0)}(X)\leq R$. By the second part of Theorem \ref{thm: Convergence measure} we have that $\mu_{1}(C^x_{-\infty,R})=e^{2\rho_{\max}R}$, where $2\rho_{\max}$ is the evaluation of the supremum of the sum positive roots $2\rho$ on the unit ball of $N_{\iota\omega_1}$. Here $2\rho_{\max}=n^2-n$, as the sum of positive roots on $\mathfrak{a}$ is the linear form:
 $$2\rho:\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda_1,\cdots, \lambda_n)\mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(n+1-2i).$$
 The unit ball of $N_{\iota \omega_1}$ is the set of elements $\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda_1,\cdots, \lambda_n)$ with $\lambda_i\geq -1$ for all $i$ and $\lambda_1+\cdots +\lambda_n=0$. The maximum is reached for $\operatorname{Diag}(n-1,-1,,\cdots,-1)\in F_{1}$.
\medskip

Finally we use the inequality of Proposition \ref{prop:Identification Selberg and Finler} to see that :
$$C^x_{-\infty,
R-\log(n)} \subset \mathfrak{C}^x_{-\infty,R}\subset C^x_{-\infty,
R+\log(n)} .$$

Hence we obtain a constant $C_{1}$ for $R=0$ that satisfies the desired inequality. The inequality for all $R$ comes from the homogeneity of the measure from Theorem \ref{thm: Convergence measure}, and the fact that for $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$, $\lambda_*h_Y(X)=h_Y(X)+\lambda$.

\medskip

For the other measures $\mu_k$, we note that $\mu_k(\mathfrak{C}^x_{0,1})$ is finite as $\mathfrak{C}^X_{0,1}$ is compact. Moreover by the uniqueness of the invariant measure, there exist $c\in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda_*\cdot \mu_k= e^{\delta_k^{(\lambda)}}\mu_k$ for all $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ acting on $\mathcal{O}_k$ via $\lambda\cdot h=h(\cdot)+\lambda$, for some $\delta_k^{(\lambda)}$. Moreover $\lambda\mapsto \delta_k^{(\lambda)}$ is continuous and $\delta_k^{(\lambda+\lambda')}=\delta_k^{(\lambda)}+\delta_k^{(\lambda')}$ for all $\lambda,\lambda'\in \mathbb{R}$, $m\in \mathbb{N}_{>0}$, hence $\delta^{(\lambda)}_k=\lambda \delta_k$ for all $\lambda$. In particular $\mu_k(\mathfrak{C}^x_{-\infty,0})$ is finite and $\mu_k(\mathfrak{C}^x_{-\infty,R})=e^{\delta_kR}\mu_k(\mathfrak{C}^x_{-\infty,0})$.

body_md:
\label{lem:3 conditionsbis}
    Let $Y_0\in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ be a horofunction and let $E\subset \mathcal{X}$ be a subset. Let $\Pi_0\cup \lbrace Y_0 \rbrace$, where $\Pi_0$ is a Poisson point process on $\mathcal{O}_1$ with measure intensity $\mu_1$. We consider the Voronoi tessellation $(\mathcal{C}_Y)_{Y\in \Pi\cup \lbrace Y_0\rbrace}$ of $\mathcal{X}$ associated to $\Pi_0\cup \lbrace Y_0\rbrace$ for the Selberg invariant \footnote{The functions we compare to build the diagram are $\mathfrak{s}(\cdot, Y)$ for $Y\in \Pi_0\cup \lbrace Y_0\rbrace$}.
    \begin{itemize} 
    \item[(i)] Suppose that $\mathfrak{s}(\cdot,Y_0)$ has linear growth on $E$ , meaning that for some $A,B>0$, for all $X\in E$:
$$\mathfrak{s}(X,Y_0)\geq A \mathfrak{s}(X,O)-B.$$

Then almost surely $C_{Y_0}\cap E$ is bounded.

\item[(ii)] Suppose that $E$ is unbounded. If $h$ is not proper and bounded from below on $E$, then almost surely $C_{Y_0}\cap E$ is unbounded.

\item[(iii)]  Suppose that $-h$ has linear growth on $E$,  meaning that for some $A,B>0$, for all $X\in E$:
$$\mathfrak{s}(X,Y_0)\leq -A\mathfrak{s}(X,O)+B.$$

Suppose also that the $1$-neighborhood $E_1$ of $E$ has subexponential volume growth, meaning that the volume of $E_1 \cap B(o,t)$ is $o(e^{\epsilon t})$ for all $\epsilon>0$. Then almost surely $E\setminus C_{Y_0}$ is bounded.
\end{itemize}

body_md:
We use again Proposition \ref{prop:Mecke} to say that one can consider a fixed horofunction $Y_0\in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ in order to prove $(i)$ and $(ii)$ or two fixed opposite horofunctions $Y_1,Y_2\in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ in order to prove $(ii)$ and check that for a Poisson point process $\Pi_0'$ on $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ with intensity $\mu_1$ the Voronoi tessellation $(\mathcal{C}_h)_{Y\in \Pi'_0\cup \lbrace Y_0\rbrace }$ and respectively $(\mathcal{C}_Y)_{Y\in \Pi'_0\cup \lbrace Y_1,Y_2\rbrace }$ satisfy these properties almost surely.

Let us prove $(i)$. The cell $\mathcal{C}_{Y_0}$ is the set of $X\in \mathcal{X}$ such that for all $Y\in \Pi_0'$ one has $\mathfrak{s}(X,Y_0)\leq \mathfrak{s}(X,Y)$. This inequality is equivalent to $\operatorname{Tr}(X(Y_0'-Y_0))\geq 0$, hence it is the intersection of $\mathcal{X}$ with linear half spaces in $S^2V$, meaning it is corresponds to a convex subset in $\mathbb{P}(S^2V)$. The fact that it has locally finitely many sides comes from the fact that for all $X\in \mathcal{X}$ and $R>0$, almost surely $\lbrace Y\in \Pi_0'\mid \mathfrak{s}(X,Y)\leq R\rbrace$ is finite, as in Proposition \ref{prop: Tessellation}.

Given $[Y_0]\in \mathcal{O}_{1}$, if we fix some basis so that its associated bilinear form is given by the following symmetric matrix $Y_0=\operatorname{Diag}(0,1,\cdots, 1)$. Now let us define $[X_\infty]=P_{Y_0}$. This symmetric matrix span the unique line of semi-positive elements $X$ so that $\operatorname{Tr}(XY_0)=0$.


Now we show $P_{Y_0}$ belongs to $\overline{\mathcal{C}_{y_0}}$. Let us assume that $y_0$ corresponds to the symmetric matrix $Y_0$. Consider the sequence $(X_k)$ in $\mathcal{X}$ corresponding to the symmetric matrices $X_k=e^{-k/n}\operatorname{Diag}(e^{k},1,\cdots, 1)$, so that $\det(X_k)=1$. This sequence clearly converges to $P_{Y_0}$ in $\overline{\mathcal{X}}$. We have $\mathfrak{s}(X_k,Y_0)=-\frac{k}{2n}+\frac{1}{2}\log (\frac{n-1}{n})$. By applying part $(iii)$ of Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditionsbis} to the sequence $(X_k)$, we see that for all but finitely many $k\in \mathbb{N}$, $X_k\in \mathcal{C}_{y_0}$ and hence the limit, which is $P_{Y_0}$, belongs to $\overline{\mathcal{C}_{Y_0}}$.

Now let us show that $\overline{\mathcal{C}_{Y_0}}\cap \partial \mathcal{X}\subset\lbrace P_{Y_0}\rbrace$. We define for $\epsilon>0$ the set $E_\epsilon\subset \overline{\mathcal{X}}\subset \mathbb{P}(S^2V)$ of elements $X\in \mathcal{X}$, such that $\operatorname{Tr}(XY_0)/\operatorname{Tr}(X)\leq \epsilon$. 
First note that if $X\notin E_\epsilon$, then $\mathfrak{s}(X,Y_0)> \mathfrak{s}(X,\mathrm{Id})+\frac{1}{2}\log(\epsilon)$. We can therefore apply part $(i)$ of Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditionsbis} to the complement of $E_\epsilon$.
This proves that for all $\epsilon>0$, almost surely there is a compact subset $K\subset\mathcal{X}$ such that $\mathcal{C}_{Y_0}\cap K\subset E_\epsilon$. Hence by considering rational $\epsilon$, we obtain that almost surely $\overline{\mathcal{C}_{Y_0}}\cap \partial \mathcal{X}\subset \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \overline{E_\epsilon}$. But this intersection contains the classes of non-zero semi-positive matrices $X$ such that $\operatorname{Tr}(XY_0)=0$, which consist only of the line corresponding to $P_{Y_0}\in \partial \mathcal{X}$ as $Y_0$ has rank $n-1$. This concludes the proof of part $(i)$. 

Now let us show part $(ii)$. For almost every pair $Y_1,Y_2$ for the measure $\mu_1$ the corresponding flags are opposite. Using Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditionsbis} part $(i)$, and the linear properness on bisectors from Lemma
\ref{lem:Proper Horofunctions Selberg} we obtain that almost surely $\mathcal{C}_{Y_1}\cap \mathcal{C}_{Y_2}$ is bounded.

\medskip

Now for part $(iii)$ Let us assume that $X\in \mathcal{X}$ corresponds the identity symmetric basis and that $Y_0=\operatorname{Diag}(0,1,\cdots,1)$ in some basis. Pick a compact neighborhood $K$ of $\mathrm{Id}$ in the space of positive symmetric matrices and let consider one parameter subgroup :$$(g_t)=(e^{-t/n}\operatorname{Diag}(e^t,1,\cdots,1))_{t\in \mathbb{R}}.$$

We define $E$ to be the union $\bigcup_{t\in \mathbb{R} }g_t\cdot K$, which is also the projective cone with base $K$ and tip $P_{Y_0}$ in $\overline{\mathcal{X}}$. This cone is a union of translates of a fixed compact set along a geodesic, and along this geodesic $\mathfrak{s}(\cdot,Y_0)$is linearly descreasing. Hence this cone satisfies the hypothesis of part $(iii)$ in Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditionsbis}. Hence almost surely $E\setminus (\mathcal{C}_{y_0}\cap E)$ is relatively compact. Hence for all $X'\in K$, the intersection of the segment $(P_{Y_0},X']$ with the convex $\mathcal{C}_{y_0}$ is a convex of the form $(P_{Y_0},X'']$. We now apply this result to a countable familly of compact sets $K$ covering $\mathcal{X}$ in order to obtain this result amost surely for any $X'\in \mathcal{X}$.

label: rem:ClosureHoroball
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ClosureHoroball}
The fact that the closure of a cell for the Selberg ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation for $\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})$ contains a unique point in the "dual"\footnote{Recall again here that the horofunction compactification for the Selberg invariant is naturally the dual Satake compactification, whose dual is the standard Satake compactification} horofunction compactification is coming from the fact that the closure of horoballs also contain a unique point in the dual horofunction compactification.

\medskip

The analog is not true for general polyhedral Finsler metrics. For instance if we consider the Finsler metric $d_{\omega_1}$ restricted to the symmetric space $\mathbb{X}_{\operatorname{Sp}} \subset \mathcal{X}$ of $\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})$, the orbit $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ is different from the case $G=\operatorname{SL}(4,\mathbb{R})$ with the same metric: a standard horofunction in $\mathcal{O}_{F_\rho}$ is given by : 
    \[ h_\omega(x) = \max_{\ell \subset \omega} b_\ell(x). \]
Here $\omega  \in \operatorname{Lag}(\mathbb{R}^4)$ and $b_\ell(x) = \left\lVert {\hat{\ell}} \right\rVert_x$.
The horoballs for $d_{\omega_1}$ contain more than one point in the compactification $\overline{\mathbb{X}_{\operatorname{Sp}}}$ induced by the standard Satake compactification: $\{ h_\omega \le 0\}$ contains all of $\mathbb{P}(\omega)$. We illustrate this phenomenon in Figure \ref{fig:LastFig}, where we show for two metrics for $G=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb{R})$ and $\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})$ the level lines on a flat of a horofunction. For $\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R})$ the blue arrows point to different points in the dual horofunction compactification, whereas for $\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb{R})$ these three arrows point to the same point in the dual horofunction compactification.


In particular the cells of the ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations in the symmetric space $\mathbb{X}_{\operatorname{Sp}}$ will also have several boundary points. For every $x\in \partial_N\mathbb{X}$ in the closure of a horoball,  we can find a sequence $(x_n)$ in the horoball converging to $x$. The ideal Poisson Voronoi tessellation associated to $\lbrace h_0\rbrace \cup \Pi_N$ will be such that infinitely many terms of our sequence belong to the cell of $h_0$ (Lemma \ref{lem:3 conditions} part (ii)), meaning that this point $x$ almost surely belongs to the boundary of this cell.
